A fascinating, if challenging, journey through evolution
I spent around 25 hours on my first playthrough of Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey, and it was a unique and memorable experience. The game focuses on survival, exploration, and evolution, letting you guide a clan of early hominids through the dangers and discoveries of prehistoric Africa.
The sense of progression is satisfying — learning new skills, adapting to threats, and gradually expanding your territory feels rewarding. The game’s open-ended approach and minimal hand-holding make discoveries feel earned, though it can be frustrating at times when survival feels punishing or progress is slow.
Graphically and atmospherically, it’s stunning. The African landscapes and wildlife feel alive, and moments of exploration are genuinely awe-inspiring. It’s not for everyone — the learning curve and pacing are unusual — but if you enjoy survival games with a focus on evolution and discovery, this is a standout experience.
👍 Recommended for patient, curious players

I really enjoyed how this game has a simple approach to it, but the human element runs deeper than expected. I am a touch conflicted about the end, though, but I think I understand the angle the developers were going for, and I think they got that part quite right.

This game is definitely worth the money, but that's in my perspective, you should absolutely try the demo first.
CUSTOMIZATION:
The customization is absolute, it feels limitless, and unlocking these parts are mostly rewarding.
COMBAT:
The combat is fun, it's not amazing or godly tier-wise, but if you learn the feel of things and get a decent build for the level, it's fun.
LEVELS:
Levels have some variety, I'm not ecstatic about the variety in levels, but It's definitely good compared to the "low bar" of gaming; this is helped with the divergence of playable levels in trees. (e.g. "STORY", or "HUNT")
DIFFICULTY:
It does feel like difficulty spikes somewhat, with several moments where I have to rethink my build, but this just means you have to think a tad bit with this game.
ONLINE PLAY:
Online play is a different story. I don't actually know how it goes down in the lobbies, but that's because not many people play it, so it's just how socially "dead" games work. I believe that if the multiplayer games are fairly similar to the main levels, it could be fun. But, I admit that I've never used multiplayer because of the lack of players.
CONCLUSION:
Overall, I give this game a very positive view, but like I said earlier, you should absolutely try the demo first, so you don't go in absolutely blind.

Lost In Vivo is a terrifying, anxiety-inducing survival horror game that caught me off guard in the best way. I first discovered it through its haunting soundtrack, and the music alone hooked me for life - ambient dread at its finest.
The game’s PS1-style graphics, claustrophobic environments, and labyrinthine sewers make every corner feel tense. I genuinely felt lost at times, constantly checking my map, and the limited FOV only added to the suspense. Chasing your dog is the premise, and while it’s emotionally relatable, the game doesn’t fully explore it - but the psychological horror more than makes up for that.
Sound design is excellent. Each creature has a distinct sound, and the silence at times is just as unnerving. Some gameplay moments stand out, like the apple puzzle and instances where the game breaks the fourth wall, though combat can feel too easy and repetitive.
The story and themes hit hard - mental health, anxiety, depression, and eating disorders are woven into the narrative in a way that’s subtle but impactful. Replayability comes from secret modes and alternate endings, though the game leaves many questions unanswered.
If you want psychological horror that messes with your mind, makes you feel genuinely anxious, and sticks with you long after finishing, Lost In Vivo is worth playing. Just be ready to feel on edge.

Oxenfree – 100% Completion Review
All achievements earned, every collectible found, all endings unlocked, full dialogue paths explored
Oxenfree is a supernatural coming-of-age story that blends naturalistic dialogue with unnerving atmosphere and narrative time loops.
Completing everything deepens the sense that you are not just shaping events, but echoing through them.
You play as Alex, a teenager on a remote island with friends, trying to enjoy a night out before everything goes sideways. A strange radio signal opens something beneath the surface, and time itself fractures. Conversations rewind, memories stutter, and the line between choice and fate begins to blur.
Dialogue is the core mechanic, and it works brilliantly.
Choices are made in real time, without pausing the flow of conversation. People interrupt. Emotions carry over. Completing all endings and paths reveals just how reactive the game can be, and how each tone shift or moment of silence creates new meaning.
The story is unsettling without resorting to jump scares.
Audio logs, spectral events, and visual glitches sell the horror. The mystery unfolds slowly, with clues hidden in both environment and repeated playthroughs. Unlocking the true ending and discovering the game’s buried layers is where the experience clicks.
Visually, it is simple but evocative. The painted backdrops contrast with sharp, minimal UI. The soundtrack pulses beneath everything, giving even quiet scenes a sense of tension.
Oxenfree trusts the player to pay attention, and rewards those who do.

I would love to see some quality of life added to this game, especially in the crafting menus (forges): A better classification, a search bar and an automated mechanic that will detect the items that exist in a certain range (inside the chests) for example. In general, this game can, with some -seemingly- easy fixes, go up 10 levels. Beyond these and a few more minor complaints, this game is amazing as it takes you on a journey to a wonderful world.
Overall, this is a unique experience that you will certainly not regret having.

M.A.S.S. Builder is a mech action RPG developed by Vermillion Digital and published by Sekai Project that places player creativity at the center of its experience. Built around customization, high-speed combat, and progression-driven systems, the game delivers a fantasy that many mech enthusiasts have wanted for years: complete control over building a personalized combat machine and taking it into battle against overwhelming threats. While it contains rough edges in some areas, M.A.S.S. Builder succeeds by understanding what makes giant robot games exciting and building its systems around player freedom rather than limitation.
Set in a future where humanity faces extinction from hostile creatures known as Quarks, the game establishes a world shaped by conflict and technological advancement. Civilization survives by developing specialized combat units called Mechanical Assault Skeleton Suits, powerful machines built specifically to fight against these devastating enemies. Players step into the role of a pilot operating within a military organization tasked with defending humanity while gradually uncovering larger mysteries surrounding the ongoing war.
The narrative itself functions primarily as a framework supporting progression rather than the central attraction. Story sequences introduce characters, establish the setting, and create motivation for continued advancement, but M.A.S.S. Builder clearly places its greatest emphasis elsewhere. The heart of the experience lies inside the garage, where players spend enormous amounts of time designing, refining, and perfecting their machines.
Customization becomes the game’s defining strength almost immediately. Very few mech titles offer the same level of freedom when it comes to constructing a personal machine. Armor pieces can be adjusted extensively, colors can be modified with significant precision, visual details receive tremendous flexibility, and cosmetic choices remain separated from statistical performance systems. This design decision proves remarkably important because players never feel forced to sacrifice appearance for efficiency.
The result creates a stronger sense of ownership over progression. A mech gradually transforms from a collection of parts into something that feels entirely personal. Whether players prefer heavily armored battlefield machines, sleek high-speed units, or designs inspired by classic science fiction and anime influences, the customization systems provide enough freedom to support a wide range of creative ideas.
The building process extends beyond visual appearance as well. Internal systems influence combat performance through upgrades and equipment choices that affect mobility, durability, offensive strength, and battlefield specialization. Different configurations encourage experimentation, allowing players to create machines designed for aggressive close-range combat, long-range support roles, balanced versatility, or highly mobile hit-and-run tactics.
Combat itself embraces speed rather than simulation realism. Battles prioritize movement and momentum, encouraging players to dash across environments, reposition rapidly, and constantly adapt to enemy pressure. Encounters rarely reward standing still. Mobility becomes a core survival skill, especially as larger enemy groups and stronger opponents begin appearing later in progression.
Weapon variety strengthens combat considerably. Different loadouts dramatically alter how battles feel, giving players opportunities to experiment with melee systems, firearms, energy weapons, missile launchers, and hybrid approaches. Pairing equipment choices with movement preferences creates meaningful strategic flexibility while reinforcing the importance of customization systems outside combat itself.
Progression follows a familiar but satisfying structure built around completing missions, gathering resources, and improving machine capabilities over time. Enemy encounters generate materials necessary for upgrades while unlockable equipment continuously expands available options. Advancement remains rewarding because nearly every improvement directly contributes toward making machines stronger, faster, or more personalized.
One of the game’s strongest accomplishments lies in how effectively it connects progression to creativity. New rewards rarely feel disconnected from gameplay goals. Unlocks directly expand possibilities rather than simply increasing numerical power. The constant flow of new components and customization opportunities creates a powerful motivation to continue advancing.
Visually, M.A.S.S. Builder succeeds where it matters most. Mechanical designs look impressive, customization details remain highly visible, and personalized machines feel satisfying to watch in motion. The anime-inspired presentation complements the setting effectively while emphasizing the fantasy of piloting powerful futuristic war machines.
The soundtrack and audio presentation support combat well without overwhelming gameplay. Weapon impacts carry satisfying weight while battlefield audio reinforces movement and combat intensity effectively. Audio design contributes positively to immersion even if it does not become the game’s defining feature.
However, M.A.S.S. Builder occasionally reveals limitations beneath its ambitious ideas. Mission structure can become repetitive during longer sessions, particularly when farming resources becomes necessary for continued upgrades. Certain balancing decisions occasionally favor specific builds more heavily than others, and some progression elements require greater repetition than ideal.
Storytelling also feels less developed compared to customization and combat systems. Narrative moments perform their purpose adequately, but players primarily interested in deeper character writing or stronger world-building may occasionally wish for greater narrative depth.
Technical roughness occasionally appears as well. Some systems demonstrate smaller inconsistencies that reveal the game’s independent development origins. None of these issues completely undermine the experience, but they occasionally prevent certain ideas from reaching their full potential.
Despite those shortcomings, M.A.S.S. Builder succeeds because it understands what makes mech games memorable. Piloting giant robots matters, but creating them matters even more. Vermillion Digital builds an experience that celebrates imagination and personal expression without restricting creativity behind unnecessary limitations.
The game delivers a satisfying combination of customization freedom, fast-paced combat, and progression systems strong enough to support long-term investment. For players who enjoy mech action games, science fiction combat, and building personalized machines capable of dominating battlefields, M.A.S.S. Builder offers one of the stronger customization-focused mech experiences currently available.

Rogue Legacy is a game I have tried and tried to like for years. I've tried getting into it in 2013 and again in 2023 but it just hasn't clicked for me. I don't like writing negative reviews and rarely do, especially for games that I can at least appreciate what the developers were going for, but this simply doesn't compare to other games in the genre. I do admit that I am not the best bad at roguelites; rarely do I beat any (besides FTL and OG Binding of Isaac). I have always enjoyed my time with most of them though. Many of these other games have a solid gameplay loop and/or a clear progression (either with unlocks or simply your skill as a player). These two factors are essential to any good roguelite, because even if they're hard and frustrating, you can still have fun amidst the failure and/or make noticeable progress.
I never felt like I could do this with this Rogue Legacy. The game's progression is so slow and dependent on good performance that you don't really get anywhere in it unless you're very good at the game. All progression (weapons, upgrades, etc.) is tied to how much gold you get in the castle. Every time you start a run though it wipes all the gold you collected previously. This means you can't save for anything and must spend it or lose it, and unless you got enough gold in your previous run to buy an upgrades (which get somewhat expensive), womp womp bye bye money. Even if you did manage to get enough gold in your previous run, most upgrades are tiny single point stat increases, making it all feel like a grindy slogfest. Now the family lineage mechanic is a neat little gimmick, but it contributes to the slow progression. After every death you get to pick from three descendents, each with specific traits that either help or severely handicap you. Some options are so bad that there is no way you're going to make it far with them. There's already so much trial and error that when you add on the way they deal with gold/upgrades, the fact that rooms are randomly generated, and how hard the game is, it's all too luck based for my liking and progress is absolutely glacial. This all would be less of a problem if the gameplay itself was fun, but it really isn't. Because of how random each run felt, I never could get a solid grasp on what I should and shouldn't be doing.

Parkasaurus is a delightfully playful twist on the classic dinosaur-park management formula, approaching the genre with charm and color rather than gritty realism. Washbear Studio clearly set out to create a game that captures the joy of building rather than the stress of micromanaging every system, and that design philosophy is felt immediately. Dinosaurs arrive in eggs rather than labs, wear silly hats, and waddle around their enclosures with exaggerated personality, giving the entire experience a cheerful, welcoming energy. Yet beneath the adorable presentation lies a thoughtful management system that asks you to balance habitat creation, guest satisfaction, staff organization, and long-term park development. It is a blend of whimsy and genuine strategy that gives Parkasaurus its distinct identity.
The core of the game revolves around designing exhibits tailored to each dinosaur’s needs. Different species require specific biomes, terrain compositions, privacy levels, and environmental elements such as shade, trees, and water. Sculpting the land with the terrain tools becomes a rewarding process: you carve hills, raise plateaus, create ponds, and decorate spaces to keep your dinosaurs comfortable. Meanwhile, you also have to ensure that visitors can actually enjoy the park—placing pathways, building cafés, installing restrooms, managing garbage systems, and setting up viewing areas that balance guest visibility with dinosaur privacy. This push and pull between creature welfare and guest entertainment adds depth without ever feeling overwhelming.
Progression is structured around research, expeditions, and egg incubation. Sending scientists into dig sites allows you to gather fossils, extract DNA, and unlock new dinosaurs. Each discovery opens up new exhibit possibilities and nudges you to expand the park in interesting ways, keeping the sense of discovery alive. Staff play a meaningful role as well: scientists, janitors, and keepers all have responsibilities that impact the park’s efficiency, and investing in their training improves overall performance. These systems create a satisfying loop of growth—research unlocks more dinos, more dinos attract more guests, and more guests provide the funds for further expansion.
Where Parkasaurus truly shines is in its relaxed pacing and creative freedom. The game never pressures you with harsh fail states or punishing economic downturns. Instead, it encourages experimentation, inviting you to build oddly shaped habitats, decorate your park with playful items, and customize your dinosaurs with a range of unlockable hats. The campaign mode is gentle and approachable, functioning more like a series of guided scenarios that teach mechanics. Sandbox mode, meanwhile, removes most constraints entirely, letting you construct the park purely according to your imagination. This emphasis on fun means that players who enjoy expressive building will find a lot to love here.
At the same time, the game’s friendly design philosophy is also its main limitation. Players who crave deep, unforgiving management challenges may find Parkasaurus too forgiving. Money is relatively easy to maintain once your park is established, and disasters or unexpected crises are rare. The late game also lacks some of the complexity seen in more hardcore simulations, which can make long-term play feel repetitive once your park is thriving. A few interface quirks—such as fiddly object placement or small text—can occasionally break the flow, though these issues never become substantial barriers.
Despite these minor drawbacks, Parkasaurus succeeds beautifully as a lighthearted, visually appealing, and surprisingly thoughtful park-builder. It captures the wonder of seeing dinosaurs in motion, gives players a wide toolbox to craft vibrant exhibits, and maintains a tone that makes experimentation inviting rather than intimidating. Its blend of strategy and creativity is engaging, and its cheerful presentation turns even routine tasks into something enjoyable. For players who want a dinosaur management game that emphasizes warmth, personality, and expressive building rather than punishing realism, Parkasaurus is an absolute pleasure to play.

Full Metal Furies is an energetic and surprisingly thoughtful action brawler that takes familiar beat-’em-up foundations and builds something far more strategic and cooperative on top of them. Developed and published by Cellar Door Games, the studio best known for Rogue Legacy, the game immediately signals that it is not content with being a simple button-mashing throwback. Instead, it blends fast-paced combat, RPG-style progression, and puzzle-like combat rules into a tightly designed experience that rewards awareness, adaptability, and teamwork. While it can be played solo, its design philosophy is clearly centered around the idea of multiple heroes working together, making it stand out within a genre often dominated by lone warriors.
The game’s world and narrative are lighthearted but purposeful, framing the action around a group of four heroines known as the Furies, who set out to challenge massive Titans threatening their land. The story doesn’t aim for epic tragedy or heavy emotional drama, but it carries a confident tone filled with humor, banter, and personality. Dialogue exchanges between characters help establish their identities and relationships, making the journey feel lively rather than purely functional. The narrative acts as a strong backdrop rather than the main attraction, giving context and momentum to the action without ever slowing the game down or overwhelming the player with exposition.
Combat is where Full Metal Furies truly distinguishes itself. At a glance, it looks like a classic side-scrolling brawler, but it quickly becomes clear that success depends on far more than quick reflexes. Each of the four Furies represents a distinct role, from close-range brawlers and defensive tanks to ranged specialists and tactical support characters. Enemies often feature color-coded shields that can only be broken by specific characters, forcing players to think carefully about positioning, target priority, and timing. This system adds a layer of strategy rarely seen in the genre, transforming chaotic encounters into structured combat puzzles that demand smart decision-making rather than brute force.
Progression systems deepen that tactical foundation. As characters gain experience, players unlock new abilities and upgrades that meaningfully change how each Fury plays. These upgrades aren’t simple stat boosts; they often alter how skills behave, enabling new synergies or playstyles that encourage experimentation. The game is generous in allowing players to respec and try different builds, which keeps progression flexible and prevents early mistakes from feeling punishing. Even failure is treated constructively, as experience and resources are retained, encouraging players to learn from mistakes rather than feel discouraged by difficulty spikes.
Full Metal Furies shines brightest in cooperative play, where its systems feel fully realized. With up to four players supported through both local and online multiplayer, the game becomes a dynamic exercise in coordination and communication. Shield mechanics, revives, and complementary abilities all come together naturally when each Fury is controlled by a different player, turning intense fights into moments of shared triumph or frantic recovery. While solo play remains viable thanks to quick character switching, it undeniably demands more mental juggling and can feel more challenging, reinforcing the game’s emphasis on collaboration.
Visually, the game embraces vibrant pixel art that is both expressive and practical. Characters are animated with clarity and personality, while environments are detailed without becoming visually cluttered. This balance is crucial during hectic battles, as it ensures enemies, hazards, and projectiles remain readable even when the screen fills with action. The art style pairs well with the game’s upbeat tone, and the varied environments help keep the long campaign visually engaging from start to finish.
There are moments where the game’s ambition can feel demanding. Difficulty spikes can be sharp, particularly for solo players or groups still learning how different characters interact. The reliance on specific character roles means that careless play is punished more harshly than in traditional brawlers, which may frustrate players expecting a more casual experience. Additionally, while the story is charming, it doesn’t evolve into something deeply memorable, serving its purpose without leaving a lasting emotional imprint.
Overall, Full Metal Furies is a standout indie action game that elevates the beat-’em-up formula through smart design and cooperative depth. Its blend of fast combat, strategic mechanics, and flexible progression makes it engaging both mechanically and socially, especially when played with others. By emphasizing teamwork and thoughtful play over raw aggression, it delivers a satisfying and distinctive experience that rewards patience, coordination, and mastery. For players looking for a brawler that offers more substance beneath its colorful exterior, Full Metal Furies is a confident and rewarding choice.

If you're after something a little different, Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is certainly that. The game doesn't hold your hand, and mistakes can and will have some pretty serious consequences, including wiping out your entire bloodline. While that might frustrate some people, I think it's part of the point and fits the idea of experiencing the early stages of human development. You really do feel like you're figuring things out for yourself.
The mechanics can however, become repetitive over time, although exploring new regions helped keep things interesting for me. The world feels large, and you definitely have the sense that you’re not at the top of the food chain. Misjudge a jump, run into a wild boar, or simply hang around somewhere you shouldn't, and you can find yourself going extinct surprisingly quickly. The evolution and scientific side of the game were particularly interesting, gradually learning new abilities and eventually evolving into a new species was cool.
100% completion did start to feel like a bit of a slog, especially when trying to get certain animals to attack each other. Overall tho, I enjoyed the concept and the experience, although I do wish we could have continued evolving all the way into modern humans.

So, if you like both relaxing experiences and exploration, this is a great game, although the price of 10€ might seem a bit high for a small walking simulator.

«Transistor» draws you in from the very first second. There are no introductions or long waits in the main menu. You pick up the Transistor and the game begins. Many things immediately catch your eye: a stunningly drawn cyberpunk world with art design that’s very soft and pleasing to the eye. The visuals aren’t overwhelming, and are undoubtedly the game’s main strength. The design holds up right through to the very end of the game.
The game runs at a maximum resolution of 1080p, but it looked good on my 1440p monitor, despite some scaling issues. You can switch the game to full-screen mode via a simple setting in Steam-Game properties (-x 2560 -y 1440).
Transistor features a very pleasant soundtrack that suits the cyberpunk genre and draws you right in. It’s not quite on a level with, say, Expedition 33, but it’s on a level with something like Hollow Knight, where a magical soundtrack is needed to complement the delicate visuals and fully immerse you in the game. What’s more, a couple of the tracks feature some lovely vocals.
As for the gameplay – things are a bit more complicated here. I can’t exactly call it good. For a game lasting 7 hours, it’s quite unique and enjoyable.
In theory, we have a whole bunch of abilities that can be combined with one another, but in practice, as soon as we acquire one of the abilities that deals the most damage, 70% of the others simply become useless.
❗Once a high-damage Function becomes available, experimenting with other combinations feels far less rewarding.
We also have a semi-active combat system here: you can always trigger your turn and choose the order of actions to deal with enemies more effectively. However, whilst your turn is recharging, the game continues in real time.
:\\Crash(), Ping(), Bounce()
I’m getting to what I consider the worst part of the game: the plot. Is there even one here…? I suppose so?
Don’t get me wrong: the narrative draws you in well, the narrator isn’t annoying right up to the end of the game and is interesting to listen to, but this game’s lore is designed for YouTube analysis videos and forum discussions, not for individual analysis of the plot. I don’t like it when a developer refuses to tell the story straight and leaves the player in the dark, failing to provide clear answers to questions and forcing the player to fill in too many gaps themselves.
❗You won’t find answers to «What?» and «Why?» in this game, especially if you skip the ability descriptions and the terminals with notes.
80% of the in-game story is contained in the notes associated with our abilities, each of which represents a specific person from Cloudbank. By using our abilities, we unlock new notes, and to be honest, reading these notes wasn’t boring, but it was rather tedious. I’d have preferred a visual narrative to this sort of thing.
The game’s atmosphere is stunning, but I wouldn’t call the plot the same. It’s far too abstract and doesn’t provide any clear answers. Some people might like that, but I don’t. The ending is a bit weak, too.

This game allows you to take control of a group of stumpy alcoholics in their stubborn efforts to avoid sobriety and lead them to greatness. Lots of memes out there are all about how "losing is fun" in Dwarf Fortress, and while that may indeed be the case, it isn't the full story, just like how the difficulty curve of Dwarf Fortress being one of the hardest games out there is also a bit misleading. To put it simply, Dwarf Fortress has an incredibly high skill ceiling, but also a low skill floor. Dig down, figure out farming, brewing, basic crafting, and tavern construction and you've got all the basics down. 975 hours in and I've barely touched the channeling tool, barely made use of water, never even touched lava, never got adamantine, have built easily a dozen capitals, many without even getting into the concepts of machines or siege weapons. There's a LOT of complexity in Dwarf Fortress that people mistake for extreme difficulty, but you need not be afraid of this as you can, and likely will, learn more and more over time. A few quick tutorials and you'll be set for your first fortress. You'll want to learn what more you can do and with each tutorial you'll get new ideas and want to- no, NEED to build bigger, better, and DEEPER. What you need in your life is below.

Although Khimera wears its influences very heavily on its sleeves, there is an undeniable amount of soul and love put into almost every aspect.
My biggest compliment is easily the gameplay. Not only is the main character great to control, but the level design compliments the fast-paced movement excellently, allowing someone who's only a few hours in to gain a good enough sense of how to speedrun through some levels (which you'll need to master if you're going for the race achievements). Items and upgrades are also done incredibly well. Unlike in Shovel Knight or Mega Man, the items you get after beating a stage don't need to be equipped and instead are either passive abilities or can be performed with a button command. Almost every stage benefits from having a specific item, whether that be from taking out enemies more easily or bolting through the stage quicker, so having items done this way gives you and your character an amazing sense of progression within the game.
This game has a great personality, and this is not only seen through the loveable character designs but through the writing, which surprisingly didn't make me want to die and actually made me chuckle a few times. I really appreciated the journal collectibles, as they were fun to hunt down while also fleshing out characters and making me connect with them more. The music and pixel art is good for the most part, and my only complaint is that the art style/sound font aren't always consistent through all areas (I love the Pumpkin Valley theme, but it feels like comes from a different game).
Suits and Sandals really impressed me here, so much so that I'll check out their entire catalogue and anything they release in the future.

This game offers a fantastic experience with an abundance of content to keep players engaged. I genuinely have no significant complaints, only a few constructive suggestions about minor issues I encountered during my playthrough.
-Lack of Late-Game Explorable Content
Exploration is a major highlight of the game, allowing you to discover new lands, trading outposts, mercenaries, and more. There are roughly 30-40 areas to explore in each cardinal direction, eventually leading to an infinite path that becomes available later on. While this feature is enjoyable, I wish there was more content to experience once you've explored all of the cardinal direction slots. When these areas are exhausted, the excitement of exploration fades, leaving only the pursuit of more land to add to your kingdom through the infinite exploration feature. I think expanding this content would greatly enhance the experience, perhaps allowing players to reset the explored cardinal areas, similar to how you can reset after you have conquered kingdoms. Adding more content related to the demon realm could also add variety and depth.
-More Purchasable Content in the Late Game
Similar to the exploration aspect, the late game suffers from a lack of purchasable content. Once you've fully upgraded your kingdom and experimented with shops and taverns, there isn’t much left to do with your wealth except continuously buying new units each turn. Adding more late-game purchases or investments could add variety and keep the game interesting.
-Keybinds for Streamlining Tedious Menu Options
After losing a significant number of troops, it's natural to want to replenish them, especially when preparing for the next attack or defense. It became quite tedious to navigate each individual menu to purchase available units like peasants, soldiers, knights, and goblins. A "buy all" button for troops, similar to the infinite land exploration button, would make this process far more efficient. The same applies to upgrading troops—being able to upgrade all newly acquired units with a single action would significantly improve the late-game flow.
For the current price point, the game is a must-buy, offering plenty of activities, adjustable difficulty, and customizable character lore. However, the content can become repetitive, and the charming but cumbersome lack of a clickable UI can be frustrating in the late game. Despite these drawbacks, I had a great time playing it and would recommend it to anyone considering it or simply looking for some enjoyable, casual fun.

Between the grapple and the shotgun, this is a pretty straightforward recipe for a rewarding, mechanical game. Enemies should most definitely be more varied in the sequel, and depending on what the developer is going for, probably more intense. If the game isn't really meant to challenge the player, rather to be more of an interactive story, then it might be fine as is, but so far I feel like this is a game that wants to make the player sweat sometimes.
All in all, this is an intro, and it's got its heart in a lot of the right places. Just maybe go a little less tryhard on the writing and a little more tryhard on the level and enemy design. Remember that the primary function of a game is to be fun to play - this game has all the right tools for fun, it just needs a more engaging playground to use them in.

I think I could consider myself a fan of Scott's work, though arguably I'm not as aware of all of it. The Desolate Hope was definitely a new experience, and an insight into how Scott makes games, writes story. I was intrigued by the game's idea - abandoned robots on another planet? C'mon man, this sounds really cool. I didn't really know what to expect, and what I got was something rather different.
The mix of game genres was an interesting touch, and kept the gameplay interesting and diverse. I really liked the models and overall look of the game - sure, it may look outdated for the so-called "today's standards", but I actually really loved it. The whole environment gave that abandoned hi-tech-ish sort of energy, and really bumped up the atmosphere.
I can't leave out the music - awesome tracks! My favourite was probably the fight music, though all of it was masterfully composed. Even if it's not made by Scott (i don't know if it is), it's still a perfect fit for the game.
The story was intriguing from the start, and kept getting more interesting as I progressed. It was mostly conveyed through dialogue, but I don't really mind it that way. Somewhere in the middle I started getting an idea where the plot was leading, but the ending was still very cool. There was apparently a controversy related to this game, but I'd be surprised if there wasn't - nowadays, people will always find something to whine about.
In conclusion: I enjoyed the game - it was nostalgic, well put-together and and interesting experience. I now am even more interested in the history of Scott Cawthon's game development.
I definitely recommend this game to everyone - especially, if you're interested in Scott's games.

Preface: Remember that this is a small indie company trying their hand in a fast, giant mech genre that is few and far in between.
Cons:
-the game has some bugs and the one that I found in particular didn't have any troubleshoot that I could find in any search engines, in here (store page,) or in their (developer's) discord.
-their response time is horrid(12+ hrs with an average of 20hrs) and apparently not as bad as when they actually address game issues as they need to be identified first and then go through the process of troubleshooting
-if you find yourself with an issue with no fix, CONGRATULATIONS! you've managed to discover something that needs fixing.
-possibly more things that one can expect from a newly released indie game
-save files and screen shots feel like playing where's waldo because they aren't located where you'd expect them.
-when customizing, you will eventually end up saying, "life would be better if I had that button". a lot. usually a 'delete' button.
-multiplayer doesn't seem to work (which is too bad, though I've seen multiplayer games on youtube so idk)
-the game will occasionally remind you that the game requires a bit of your patience
-as great as the customization is, you will eventually hit a wall and when you do, you'll be sorely disappointed. it's not game breaking but it'll leave you hoping that, "they would add it to the game in the future".
-it's a very new game
Pros:
-this game moves more like AC1. no quickboosts or overboosts. you can move fast without (realistically) turning your yourself (the pilot) into mush inside the cockpit. if you're more into that or don't mind not having breakneck speeds, then you'll like how MASS moves.
-the customization has to be the highlight of the game. I find myself losing far too much time MASS BUILDING and the more time you spend on it and discover more ways to custom your machine, the longer and more MASS you'll build (if you're into designing your machine)
-even if you're not into building and would only tolerate it to recreate just about ANY character (mobile suits, armored cores, NEXTs, ranger zords, GUYVER, etc.,) you have a very powerful tool at your disposal to get very close to the desired model.
-the devs have their own discord and will eventually address you personally. you'll have to remember that they live in south east Asia and is a small dev team so if you're expecting a quick chat at your whims, you'll just get annoyed (ask me how I know). they are trying and I appreciate the effort.
-it's a very new game
How the game feels:
-machine speed falls somewhere between the realism of Battletech/Mech Warrior/Mech Commander(typically tops at 150mph) and a flight simulator using a slower moving aircraft (ave 300-350mph) without any sudden, short boost of speed that exceeds normal function of the boosters, lending to a more fluid, flat speed combat
-combat honestly feels more like a beat em up. you can construct a machine with a varying distribution of your armour's weight (which will affect your speed), fire power (lighter weapons are faster, heavier weapons hit harder. the amount of resourcers that they consume also reflects their singular hit potential. all of that are enhanced by how you've distributed your 'talent points' which is based on the three major facets of your machine that will ultimately determine how the machine ends up playing. basically, you can specifically target attributes to make the machine play in a way that YOU would personally find fun.
other features:
-you have plenty of space to make plenty of builds.
-photograph mode allows you to showcase your the MASS you've constructed to do up to 40 poses (if I remember correctly) and to one of the many different backdrops. as far as I know, this is unique to this game only (if we're talking about games of the genre.) let's be honest now, you didn't spend all those hours painstakingly constructing your machine only to see one side of your of it on the cutscene and mostly just it's back during gameplay. you are determined to recreate, "that pose" from, "that anime/manga/show/movie"... whatever might that be. every piece you've resized, reshaped, and put in place is a step closer to a wicked drip screenshot. it'll be your desktop wallpaper.

Revisiting 'Braid': A Timeless Odyssey in Gaming
Over a decade has passed since "Braid" graced our screens, setting the gaming world ablaze with its surreal, cerebral, and retrograde charm. In an era dominated by blockbuster releases, this indie gem stood out as a critical darling, instantly catapulting its creator, Jonathan Blow, into millionaire status.
What made "Braid" such a standout? Well, it arrived at the perfect moment. As an Xbox Live Arcade exclusive, it marked a shift towards downloadable content and the rise of independently developed games. It was an era where video games were becoming more than just discs you bought at a store - they were evolving into digital experiences you downloaded onto your console.
"Braid" was not just a game; it was a statement about what video games could be. It introduced players to Tim, a seemingly ordinary protagonist, clad in a business suit. Tim had a unique ability: he could manipulate time, reversing it whenever he wished. Death was no longer a threat; instead, the challenge lay in using this power to solve intricate puzzles across 38 levels.
The story in "Braid" starts simply: Tim is on a quest to rescue a princess. However, it's the climax that elevates this game from a puzzler to a thought-provoking narrative. When Tim finally reaches the princess, the game rewinds, revealing that she had been fleeing from him all along, setting traps to deter his advances.
The interpretation of this twist varies. Some see it as commentary on toxic masculinity, while others delve into deeper meanings, like the creation of the atomic bomb. Blow, the enigmatic developer, refuses to clarify the game's message, leaving players to decipher it themselves.
Blow's reluctance to provide definitive answers is admirable. He expects players to solve the game's puzzles, and the story's meaning is the most significant puzzle of all. This obscurity is one of the game's most intriguing aspects.
In my view, the straightforward explanation - a commentary on the way video games often diminish female characters and how male gamers perceive themselves as heroes in selfish narratives - holds significant weight. It's a reflection on the gaming culture that feels even more pertinent today.
"Braid" excels because its themes are interwoven with its gameplay, deconstructing video games and gamers themselves. Yet, Blow's insistence on telling gamers they've misunderstood the game might be its chief flaw. In the realm of video games, individual experiences reign supreme. Players interpret games differently, and that's part of the beauty.
Ultimately, "Braid" challenges us to accept that players won't always see games as developers intended. And that's a puzzle worth embracing.

If you like settlement building, task management, and having to provide and create your own resources, animals, and buildings to survive you will enjoy this game. Now, I will say I do not find this game "Easy". It may be easier for some than others. I have played for 197 hours, and just today marks me making it into the Iron Age. I could have progressed sooner, but I kept waiting because I was having a hard time with raiders during the Copper Age, and/or freezing, starving populations during winter - lack of food. My biggest hurdle I personally feel makes this game take longer and harder is the map. I can hold a decent settlement between 80-120 villagers, so far. This took a lot of practice, sustainable farming, and resources. I did have several raider attacks that killed 20-40 villagers. However, with reinforced, and better walls, and better weapons it is easier to fight off the raiders. Having a higher population does give advantages to high raider pop attacks. If your village has too few people, they can be overcome easily. With having a higher population you have to have the food to sustain a higher population. I do still fish, farm, and have farm animals. You do not want to progress too quickly - or too slowly - because it is not sustainable, because you don't want to have too little people and too small a village that a raid attack kills your entire settlement. However, if you don't have enough food during winter, straw, and grain, your population will struggle, and your animal population will die off due to starvation. Further into the game its not that big of a deal, with enough crops and various types of grain as long as you don't lose your entire flock of animals - you should be okay and they will reproduce - if you have room to house them. You can set limits to your animals. Fishing through every season is very important. Hunting through most of the game is beneficial. For XP points, and food, and skins. Once you have farming - can sustain a decent herd of animals - the animals get slaughtered when they are older. Cows and goats produce milk. Horses and Donkeys can pull carts. Cows and horses can pull plows. So that your people are not manually farming the lands each season. Sometimes crops get sick - and you may lose a big portion. So a variety of crops is needed. Crops that produce straw are needed to feed the animals throughout the winter. Before stone masonry, you upgrade to straw buildings - and it's a PITA to have enough straw to sustain the buildings and sustain the animals. My pet peeve is space - the mountains get in the way of building a nice and easily defendable settlement, yet you still want to be close to mine resources - and close to water to fish, and have land open for hunting. I did not want to progress to the other challenges without first completing Continental Dawn Challenges. I have completed 9/10. I have not built a Cairn. I range around 90-120 people - so to complete the last step of this challenge I need to expand further. I have only played the Northlands for a few minutes at this point in the game - I will work on completing Northlands, and Ancient Warriors after I have finished all 10 milestones for Continental Dawn. Overall, it's not a super complicated game, but it does require resource management, building management, and a lot of patience in my opinion. I am not sure if there are enough Megaliths left of this part of the map to complete a Cairn- I built several megaliths and statues, other buildings to help with prestige, and have a 92% welfare - 601/1000 prestige currently. Using different types of megalith, funerary structures, and such. I'll have to see if I can find enough resources on this map to complete the Cairn, with what I already have, or take down some structures that already exist. I have a Dolmen built but not a Cairn.

The Howler makes a strong first impression, thanks to its stunning, hand-painted visuals. Inspired by actual landmarks found in Vilnius, Lithuania, classically-trained artists lovingly crafted each bit of steampunk scenery. Blueprints, concept art and ancient landscape sketches come together to create a beautiful environment full of wonder. Fictional imagery also dots the land, allowing the developer to do more than simply reproduce absolute reality. In one particularly noteworthy moment, you'll encounter an enormous wolf-shaped structure, complete with bloodstained maw. Eventually, you descend into its gullet and find the maze of machinery that is Vilnius' underworld.
You might well be wondering if there's any substance to back up The Howler's style. The answer, honestly, is yes. But there's not enough of it...
In simple terms, The Howler is a 2D hot air balloon simulator of sorts. By holding the left mouse button, your balloon ascends. You have little control over horizontal movement, and must therefore make use of the wind. Arrows on the left side of the screen inform you of the wind's current direction and velocity. There are multiple currents available in each stage, typically alternating in direction. That's helpful because it means that if you screw up and need to head back the way you came, all you must do is rise or plummet and catch an adjacent gust that blows in the opposite direction. Of course, you still must work within a time limit, but each course grants you a generous few minutes at a time.
The typical objective in a stage is to land at a goal point highlighted by flashing green lights. Doing so can prove tricky, since some obstacle courses don't leave much room for error. Thankfully, the first stage grants you plenty of leeway, so you can fuss with the mechanics and eventually become acclimated. likelihood that you'll pop your envelope is pretty slim. Later on, though, the campaign frustrates your efforts with jagged edges and mine-like automatons. You'll need to plan ahead in order to properly angle your ride while in motion, and you'll have to rely also on some trial and error. For instance, one stage pits you against several airborne foes. A wide overhead gap might compel you to sail over the opposition's heads, but that turns out to be a losing strategy. Through experimentation, you'll eventually discover that ducking beneath them is surprisingly more effective.
The Howler's toughest challenges were among my favorites. There's one that drove me nuts, but I loved it for that. Your itinerary includes nabbing a package off the ledge of a tower. You then must ascend and reverse your direction to drift away from the building. Finally, you swoop around toward the structure again, hopefully approaching at just the right angle to finally fly past it. At the construct's apex, the wind suddenly shifts direction and tends to blow you off course. If you hit it at the correct trajectory with fair momentum, you should climb over the roof and glide past it. Most of the time, though, your basket catches on the corner of the zenith and the breeze carries you away from the finish line. Then you can either throw yourself out of the balloon in irritation, or dust yourself off and try again.
A few stages later, there's an underground region where you must descend an old shaft while avoiding sharp architecture along its perimeter. On top of that, there's a strange spigot dropping hefty balls that will drag you into a killing pit if you collide with them. Once you've reached your descent's lowest point, you must glide to the right and press a button using your envelope, then retreat before the current throws you into a pointed object. The button you hopefully pressed will have activated a timed gate that doesn't open all the way, so you still have to be wary of piercing bars that dangle from the ceiling. This trial had me sweating buckets, but the relief that came with my eventual victory was a worthwhile reward.
I'm thankful that The Howler's collision detection is stable. I can't say that I've ever been screwed over during any of its hairy ordeals. I scraped against more than a few keen surfaces and managed to come out alive. Any time I failed an exercise, it was due to a malfunction on my end and not faulty mechanics.
Although The Howler features sound physics, a fair difficulty balance, occasional entertainment and a gorgeous art style, it isn't a particularly fulfilling experience. Its campaign offers a mere sixteen levels, one of which is an unlockable bonus mission where you command an ornithopter. I'm also disappointed by the brevity of each stage. I would have thought that some chapters near the campaign's conclusion would become quite elaborate, but they never do. Many of them are short, straightforward flights with a few special tasks to complete along the way. For instance, one course requires you to destroy all of the nearby automatons using bombs. In another case, you pursue a car while avoiding obstacles. After that, you repeat the same level in reverse, except now you have to destroy the automobile before it eludes you.
Short video games are not an issue, of course. What irks me is that The Howler sports a neat core concept that could have been better explored, but its fleeting campaign doesn't allow sufficient time for that to actually occur. Why not include more complex levels, or allow players to utilize a variety of aircraft? I'm sure the developers could also have introduced a new feature every now and then, to shake things up a bit. Unfortunately, The Howler departs the minute you've finally grown comfortable with it, and leaves you desiring more content.
At the same time, asking for additional content may be begging for punishment. I can only hope that the development team avoids pumping The Howler full of filler, should it ever decide to extend the campaign. For now, you thankfully have a decent, untarnished 60-minute romp that will simultaneously delight you and leave you wanting much more.

Came back to this game after 2-3 years since launch and it is a completely enhanced game. So many major updates.
Honestly I've played almost every deck builder steam has to offer and this is the best one tied with STS, Monster Train, and now Ratropolis. 6 different classes each with 2 subclasses, each class deck and class leader plays incredibly uniquely. There are many different ways to build each class and its just insanely fun figuring out how to get each deck running in a broken combo to beat the game. And trust me you will need to do something broken to beat the game because its HARD. Each run is such a fun challenge and it feels extremely well balanced, easy beginning, intermediate middle, and really hard lategame. They've made every class feel like a unique puzzle to solve in many interesting ways.
Runs are about 60 minutes long and you start crafting your deck up from scratch and also building a town with your deck. Enemies come in waves and you can either defend with guys and buffing your guys or with towers(mainly builder class). A new fun pollution mechanic since I've played where you can increase the difficult I believe 20 times, and if you beat a run making it to wave 30 you can go endless and continue to have fun.
I think the main takeaway of what makes this game unique and deserve to be praised along with STS, or MT is 2 things; balance, and unique classes. The challenge in every run is there, and feels balanced, and is very very fun to see if you make it to the end. Alongside the balance each class feels extremely unique with their own radically different playstyle, and the amount of smart design that goes into being able to make that is very impressive.
I hope the team who made this game makes more games because they are capable of making incredible quality and I would love to see what they do on the next game, even if its not a sequel.

The Gnorp Apologue starts strong enough, but eventually settles into a grind that feels more tedious than rewarding. The core loop could be much more satisfying if progression were tuned down by 25% or more. As it stands, following guides feels like the most practical way to finish the game and move on rather than experimenting naturally.
The design philosophy is especially confusing: the game explicitly encourages you to participate but makes your clicks ineffective, and then asks to minimize it and let currency accumulate in the background, despite not being a mobile or free-to-play title. This approach makes the active gameplay feel oddly secondary if not non-existent.
The Gnorps are charming, but there is essentially no story to carry the experience, and the prestige perks are not compelling enough to sustain interest or encourage much experimentation after the initial novelty wears off.
It is not a bad incremental game, but it's not near the top of my favorites - and I doubt it will be near yours either.

Rogue Legacy 2 builds on the clever foundation of its predecessor by expanding the idea of hereditary progression into a rich, mechanically diverse roguelite that blends fast-paced action with deep customization. Every time a character falls in battle, a new descendant steps up to continue the family legacy—each with unique traits, randomized stats, and one of many unlockable classes. These traits can range from comical quirks like upside-down vision or flatulence, to more serious gameplay modifiers that impact damage or mobility. The system not only adds variety but also keeps every run feeling fresh, and the incentive of gold bonuses for choosing more difficult traits creates an interesting risk-reward dynamic.
The game features a wide roster of character classes, each of which introduces entirely new combat and movement mechanics. Whether you’re playing a nimble Ranger who crafts mid-air platforms or a Boxer who builds momentum through combo chains, each class has a distinct feel that demands different strategies. As you progress, the combat becomes more layered, requiring smart positioning, cooldown management, and quick reflexes. The addition of class-specific mastery levels gives even more reason to rotate through characters rather than sticking to a favorite, encouraging experimentation and growth over time.
Exploration takes place across a series of visually distinct biomes, from lush forests to eerie caverns and ruined towers. These areas are gated behind heirloom trials, which function as mini-dungeons designed to test your platforming and combat skills. Unlocking a new ability like double-jump or air-dash not only opens up new paths in future runs but also enhances the fluidity of movement, turning the early, grounded gameplay into something far more agile and dynamic. The castle itself is procedurally generated each run but remains logically connected, giving a sense of familiarity even within its ever-changing walls.
Progression outside of runs is just as satisfying. Gold earned during expeditions can be spent on upgrading your family estate, unlocking new character classes, stat boosts, passive abilities, and useful NPCs. This meta-layer adds long-term purpose to each attempt, whether successful or not. There's also a Soul Shop that allows you to unlock permanent bonuses using a separate currency earned through optional combat challenges. For players looking for a more tailored experience, House Rules provide a welcome layer of customization, letting you tweak everything from enemy health to game speed, which makes the game approachable for a wide range of skill levels.
While platforming and movement feel smooth for the most part, certain platforming rooms can be a source of frustration. These challenge areas often require pinpoint precision, and the game’s weighty physics combined with the varying size and speed of different classes can make them feel inconsistent. Still, the frustration is usually balanced by the sense of accomplishment when you finally clear a particularly difficult obstacle or puzzle room.
Visually, Rogue Legacy 2 shines with a vibrant and expressive art style that moves away from pixel graphics in favor of hand-drawn backdrops and 3D character models. The aesthetic is both whimsical and dramatic, matching the game’s blend of humor and high-stakes action. Each area has a unique personality, with strong audio and soundtrack work to back it up. The music during heirloom trials and boss encounters, in particular, stands out as thematically powerful and immersive.
Though it may take some time to fully unlock all its systems, Rogue Legacy 2 proves itself to be one of the most well-rounded and rewarding entries in the roguelite genre. It balances moment-to-moment gameplay with long-term progression beautifully, rewarding skillful play while also respecting the time of players through meaningful meta-upgrades. The sheer amount of content, combined with polished mechanics and a commitment to variety, makes it a standout experience. For anyone who enjoyed the original or is seeking a roguelite that constantly evolves with each run, Rogue Legacy 2 is a masterfully crafted successor that more than lives up to its lineage.

The game is quirky and takes some getting used to, but it's a lot of fun... for a while.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend the game in its current state due to the lack of optimization of the physics which makes the game unplayable and, as another reviewer put it, there's more unnecessary friction with game mechanics than challenge.
My friend and I started a new game after the 1.0 release and have been enjoying it. We built several vehicles, each with different uses, built an auto-gardener that harvests, plants, and waters 863 plots of soil along, and built a simple elevator to easily access the garden. We'd just reached the underground and were excited for new equipment and build possibilities. The lag had gotten worse and worse over time, but we apparently crossed some sort of threshold and now the physics have started freaking out. We tried various physics setting to no avail. We can't even use our vehicles any more, the elevator slumps over sideways, and we dare not try the auto-gardener.
The foundation of the game is to engineer cool contraptions using physics, but it breaks after a few builds and makes the game unplayable.
Until the devs optimize the physics, I suggest refraining from playing this game very extensively.
Other issues:
There's also no dedicated server, which is ridiculous.
Trashbot is a bullet hell boss which doesn't belong in this type of game. If I wanted to play a bullet hell shooter, I'd play a different game. You can defeat him easily by building a platform above the floor, so at least there's that.
The grind is also too much. The player can make everything except Component Kits, which are probably the most important resource the player needs. Some robots *might* drop one when destroyed.
There's apparently no way to deconstruct crafted items back into their component parts.
When a piece is destroyed it's simply gone rather than deconstructed into its component parts.
Seeker Bot is initially a really cool idea -- a giant, untouchable machine that can easily destroy the player and anything the player has built -- but you quickly realize the bot is just annoying and doesn't really seem to serve a purpose other than to hassle the players and force them to shelter until the bot passes.

If you like Supergiant's games, you'll definitely like this.
I got this game sometime after playing the demo for The Pale Beyond, but only played it long after playing Pyre, which I greatly enjoyed.
Onto the meat of the review.
LEGEND: love (╋), like (+), neutral (~), dislike (-), abhor (—)
╋ MUSIC; Downbeat acoustic soundtrack with vocals. My favorite track is "There Is No Bad Weather".
╋ VISUALS; 2D Graphics look amazing. The use of colors, parallax, linear motions, and reuse of similar sprites, is as beautiful as it is impressive.
╋ STORY; Themes of trade-off, limited agency, thanatology, perspective, normalcy bias, loss aversion.
╋ UI/UX; Spacebar, Enter, and Numpad Enter, all forward text. Many indie text-based games focused on story-decisions neglect to do this, which is hugely important for comfort and usability.
╋ UI/UX; I appreciate the quality and consistency of texts descriptive of character abilities and such. They are frontloaded with "how" followed by "what", very succinct.
╋ COMBAT; One thing Banner Saga has, which I love, is low numeric values. Into the Breach also has this.
+ STORY/VISUALS; On the map, you can read descriptions about places and roads. It doesn't get much use, and it's not necessary, but it's really awesome that the option is there. It makes the world feel more alive.
+ ECONOMY; Resting spends Supplies which you find, are gifted, or buy with Renown. "Renown" is the exchange currency you get by defeating enemies in combat. This was never an issue, and in fact, I found it a fun, interesting, smooth and "unproblematic" piece of design.
∽ COMBAT; I saw a reviewer claim the "last boss is broken after 10 years" and proceed not to qualify how. I had zero issues with the last boss, and everything proceeded smoothly. I saw another claim it was "obnoxiously difficult", this was false, at least for my playthrough. It seems that the game's design might have balancing/consistency issues.
∽ COMBAT; Your health is also your damage. I've sometimes wondered what it might be to have a system like that, but I always concluded it's a bad idea to deal less damage the less health you have. It's an extremizing mechanic. It's way harder, I dare say impossible, to pull of a "clutch" win when you're at low health. It works just fine here, it's not a problem.
∽ TIME; I was ready to play for 100hs, but my playthrough was around 15-16 hours.
∽ STORY; I had expected that characters could die in combat, but this is false. They can only die in story decisions, or else, when a combat encouter is explicitly relevant for a high-stakes situation. When a character loses in combat, they become injured, and need to rest for a few days.
- UI/UX; The game autosaves (quick slot) after every decision, and after every place (ordinary slot). I take two problems here: (1) this does nothing against save scumming, and (2) you have zero control over when to save. So, the player loses control over saving, and it does not even prevent savescumming. The saving system is actively detrimental.
- STORY; The introduction into the world of Banner Saga is a little confusing. Characters are introduced without their names, and without you even seeing them for a while, since it's only narration. It's unclear if the narrator is someone, or not really anyone. After you begin playing as Ubin, this mostly subsides, but it could have been better.
- STORY; I was expecting more swaps of perspective throughout. Instead, you play a little as Ubin, then a little as Hakon, and most of the game is centered on Rook. This would've been a neutral point, but the game literally opens by telling you that perspective-taking will be a huge deal; you are setup to be disappointed.
- UI/UX; The map takes too long to load. I would have used it more if it wasn't for this.
- UI/UX; GUI is inconvenient when it comes to accessing/leaving Combat Training, as well as (un)equipping the gear of characters, and especially when you wanna do that to someone who is currently apt for a level-up.
- UI/UX; Some of the stats are unexplained. I didn't know what "REST" is, or what "CRIT CHANCE" meant, and now that I've finished the game, still do not know.
- STORY; At least in this first game, I disliked how the approach to and use of divinity. As soon as you begin, you are told "the gods are dead" . It isn't clear what significance this has in the world, or those who live in it. There are "godstones", monuments to the gods. Throughout, you uncover a little more about the significance, but it's very little indeed. The only person who seems to care is Ubin, who is terrifically old, and even then, doesn't seem to care much. Characters mostly are ambivalent, or plainly oppositional. This theme is underexplored and underutilized. It feels more of a mundane reflection of the time period this was written, and less anything substantial for the world and story. I loved visiting the godstones, they are clearly meant to be of great, great significance, and that should be reflected more generally. The end of the game almost seems to foreshadow that this will become more relevant. I'm hoping this is improved in the future games I have not yet played.
- STORY/GAMEPLAY; Yrsa died in my playthrough. I don't care that this happened, as I was not invested in her, but the way it happened was awfully contrived: she suggests an attack which uses fire on a forest. If you do this, by the end, she vanishes, is presumed dead, and Ludin blames you for her disappearance. Gunnulf is a character who I had to go out of my way to ensure he lived. If he dies, it's like nobody gives a ♥♥♥♥. Your character is more worried about the "treasure now at the bottom of the valley". Regardless, the decision sequence in which he may die is totally out of nowhere. You're traveling, and what should've been an ordinary decision about the caravan or whatever, is instead HIGHLY IMPORTANT!!!!!!!!! His death is so contrived, there is only one way to save him, you are practically forced to savescum and brute-forcedly exclude decisions.
— UI/UX; In case you accidentally skip something you did not mean to, there is no text log for you to view past messages.
— UI/UX; The character screen GUI is majorly whack. It is designed as if it were a mobile game UI. There is a Hint button you must press to get explanations for things on the screen, but instead of the descriptive tooltips being shown during mouseover, EVERYTHING is shown at once, which is horrifically bad for anyone trying to absorb new information. Not everything is explained either, mostly just the stats.
— COMBAT; By far, my biggest issue is that you can't undo movement actions. When Acting as a character, the first thing you do is Move, during which there are three steps in time: (1) before selecting a tile, (2) after selecting but before confirming, and (3) after confirming. If you're in step 2, or in step 3, you can't return to step 1. in many other strategy games, such as Into the Breach and the iconic Advance Wars, you can, yes, do this, but not here. In the negative sense of the word, this is archaic; providing neither enhancement, joy, nor challenge to the game. Additionally, contrast this with the fact this same 1-2-3 step process applies to Attacking, which you do after Movement, EXCEPT here, you can return to step 1 during step 2. You can't do that from step 3, but that is expected for attacks.
At one point in my playthrough, I thought about why Banner Saga isn't much spoken about, and concluded that just as in movies, games like this — 2D, animated, story-heavy, all around artistic skill — are affected by the technologist-photorealist slop culture we've been having since the 2000s CGI boom.
The games and studios that are, such as Supergiant themselves, are exceptions to this.

Learning about the protagonist and her relationship with her family and others is of course the highlight of the game. It's an interesting game at that, but on replays I just feel that the story is a bit unimaginative. It's also an entirely lonesome experience.
But credit where credit's due, this game did pave the way for more interesting indoor walking sims like What Remains of Edith Finch.
I still recommend Gone Home to this day as a piece of walking sim history. This is part of where it all began, and if you enjoy walking sims this is a must!

Some games are great, and some stay with you long after you've finished them. And then there's this.
I originally played this on PS4 back in 2019, revisited it on Switch in 2022, and have now completed it for the third time. This is the first time I've managed to get 100% completion so I've come out a little smug.
The premise is simple enough: you're tasked with investigating a damaged ship and piecing together the fates of its missing crew. But the way in which you go about your deductions is *chef's kiss* and I've had a hard time finding puzzle games that truly leave the entire game, and its solutions, in your hands. There's no hand holding whatsoever. Only what you can observe, piece together, and then that sweet dopamine hit when a seemingly insignificant detail finally clicks into place (looking specifically at you 4x Chinese Topmen).
The art style is instantly recognisable, the sound design is superb, and the entire experience is meticulously crafted around the central mystery. Almost every discovery feels earned, and correct deductions feels like a genuine achievement. Few others games can match the satisfaction of finally connecting the dots and realising you've figured something out entirely on your own, with no guidance, or hints.
What has impressed me the most though is this game remains worth revisiting despite having definitive answers to the mystery, which is something very few detective games can say, and I think that says a lot about the strength of the games design.

This is the first thousand hour plus idle game I've completed (of several). These are difficult to review, I'm discovering, because most of what is important in video games is not very important for idlers.
The graphics are fine. The sounds might have been okay but I heard them once, a long time ago, and never again. The creatures are cute and the gameplay is simple and relaxing.
You know what you're getting into with these games. They don't respect your time, of course, but that's the point.
The guild system here is interesting and fairly unique among idlers, but in practice I found it to be more cumbersome to deal with the systems with others than to just run my own personal guild.
I guess the only thing that really requires and deserves discussion is the monetization of the game, which I would categorize as simultaneously the best and worst possible monetization I have seen. You know what we are dealing with here: the purchase of an intermediary currency which is never quite enough to buy anything on its own due to the prices of both the gems and the items.
The game does have one outright purchase (without gems) that doubles all of your income forever. It's not expensive and it helps. I imagine this as the purchase price of the game, and I was willing to pay.
The rest of the monetization is objectively the worst, because everything costs so much. But, it's subjectively the best for the same reason! Let me explain (and my currency is USD). You earn a good amount of currency just by playing the game. Towards the end, an average once-a-day pop in could easily net me $5 or more in currency. On the other hand, the prices for things continue to increase. I had a mercenary that survived way past the level 25 mark (which was required for an achievement) and when she died, it would have cost me nearly three million dollars (in my USD currency) to ressurect her. She also could have died within minutes again after resurrection (it's random). I'm not exagerrating. You would actually have to be a millionaire (at least in American currency) to be able to pay that cost. These two factors together cause any rational, sane person to never want to spend any money in this game (beyond the initial doubler price). So, in that aspect, I feel that the monetization works perfectly as advertised.
Thanks for coming to my idle review. I know these aren't the most exciting.

Oh and despite what people say, it's maybe a quarter on land at the most (I didn't build a single thing on land other than beacons and the vehicle thing I won't spoil).
If you enjoyed Subnautica 1, get this game. I found it even less scary. It's a full game, but started as DLC so it's technically a smaller map (feels denser to compensate). Subnautica 1's map was so big that I found out at the end how I'd somehow skipped 2 whole biomes by pushing my luck. The new vehicle(s) and wildlife are both weird and fun. I played on "Freedom" difficulty to avoid worrying about food and drink, and am glad I did. I did the whole food+drink rigmarole in Subnautica 1 to prove I could; half way through you solve hunger+thirst and it's just a nagging issue taking up slots. No achievements are tied to difficulty, and they never soft lock out (game explicitly tells you when you hit the end 'point of no return').
Waiting a year and a half since finishing Subnautica 1 was definitely the right call, this game just scratched that itch nicely without getting too long. They made some attempts to help guide you through with series of flashing lights or single HUD markers for *some* content, but if you're min/ maxing for achievements, videos on the locations of things do help. I really wanted all the fragments/ upgrades, and even with guides it was challenging at times.
Anyway, I always give tips in my reviews, but mostly assumes you know Subnautica 1 gameplay:
Still only has the one save slot, so save often but only when you know you're truly safe. There's no point to playing Hardcore difficulty, in every other mode dying will only cost you almost everything you've gained since last exiting a vehicle/ base (it will randomly keep 1 item). The dropped stuff possibly falls where you died, but rolls away pretty quickly.
You only need one main base (Twisty Bridges) and just build it near the surface. Be sure to start it with platforms for way more stability than you think you'll need (because you will).
When an item is in your quickbar, use R to swap batteries (save the dead ones, you can recharge them eventually).
Hold off on guides as long as you can. F1 to see coordinates on your screen... they are in the order of: East is positive, Depth, and North is positive (in that order).
Scanning rooms are OP. You can make mini-bases that are a multipurpose room (with some kind of power generation) connected to a scanner room. Know that scanner rooms can only connect on one side, so if it's refusing to place scroll up/ down to rotate (also look out for yellow things blocking it and that it's far enough away). Building these below your swimming ability allows for easy access to late game resources. HUD scanner chip is worth it (goes on your stuff like armor), cameras are not.
I never needed torpedoes, seems like a waste of resources.
I never needed a land base, didn't even try. But do carry a flare and several beacons when you hit the biggest land section.
Don't use the numpad to launch the land vehicle, always right click to drop it straight out of inventory to avoid clipping glitches.
