The most perversely designed action economy in any tactical game I've played. Killing enemies is actively bad for you. I'm not exaggerating.
Turns strictly alternate between sides regardless of unit count. 10 vs 2? Each of their units acts five times before your last unit moves. Combine that with HP = Damage - a unit at 8hp deals 8, at 1hp deals 1. You can already see the obvious glaring problem from this: a near-dead enemy is basically a wasted enemy turn. Kill it and the slot collapses since their healthy units now cycles faster against you. The optimal play is to wound enemies close to 1 HP and leave them there as time-wasters. Yes, really its that bad.
Armor makes it worse. Armor reduces the incoming damage equal to its value. A unit with 10 armor and 2 hp will need 11 incoming damage to take 1 damage. To reduce it, you can do targeted armor attacks that deal a flat 1–2 regardless of who's swinging — so wounded units can still chip armor, but nobody crushes it quickly - no matter the hp. A fresh enemy can need 5+ turns of poking before you threaten their HP. Meanwhile their HP damage scales with their HP, so a full-health unit hits like a truck. Picture one arriving late: your team is battered at 2/9, you need half a dozen turns to crack their armor, and they one-shot your guys in the meantime. "Cleaning up" their weakened allies just hands the fresh monster more turns. If you wouldn't kill them, you could've killed the new unit before it got its second turn in. The whole system punishes every instinct a tactics game has ever trained you to follow
There is a lot more to the game, but to me it simply doesn't matter. That this foundational design got all the way is baffling. Nothing to see here, move on.

GRINDING! There is grinding in this game, however it is not boring grinding. The game encourages you to fight and gather EVERYTHING!!! When you defeat an enemy it has a respawn timer so you can't farm the same location like you typically would.

bonus. So I suggest using one at a time to get the tier faster.
THE CHARACTERS: I love them all. I don't know what else to say. There is an insane amount of character growth from Pieberry, but she isn't the only one that grows in this story.

It's solid game and for someone who has had a fascination with especially the Stone Age for a long time I think they got a surprising amount of realism in there for being a game.
The scale of the game is somewhere between "big colony sim" and "small city builder". Every villager is unique with their own name, age, lifespan, and equipment but they don't really individually matter as "characters". The building placement is not true gridless but offers enough variations you still end up with lifelike villages.
There is a lot of content in the game as you progress from hunter-gatherer to the early iron age with plenty of upgrades along the way. It is very satisfying to watch your people grow from a few hide tents and people drying meat by a river, scraping hides with flint tools etc to a bustling iron age village with livestock and varied agriculture. Also the military aspect develops from half-naked dudes chucking bone-tipped spears out in the open to warriors with swords, shields and chain mail strategically guarding choke points in stone wall systems.

I do recommend the game... but not with such fondness.
There is something about the pacing of all Klei Games that doesn't vibe with me.
I love their art style, and the base gameplay is solid.
But the way these games constantly throw threats at you, making you just do same farming/collecting task over and over again just to survive, making slow progression (I'm sure I'll get better over time)... I always find it difficult to come back to the game.
Had very similar thing happening with Klei's oxygen game as well.
I had much more fun with DST where there is direct progression, and more chaos happening due to the nature of co-op. But for single player experience, the game felt too slow for me. Oh, and dying and ending a 5+ hour run, simply because you didn't know what was coming next, definitely is not a feeling that I enjoy. This would have been fine if a run was 1 hour-ish run, but this is a bit much. I simply don't have this much time to study the game.

This is generally a good game with a few problems. (no spoilers in review)
You have to explore a number of scenes on a doomed ship, and figure out exactly what happened to each crew member. Each scene gives a bit of the puzzle, and put together you can figure out the whole picture.
The graphics are, IMO, amazing, but I certainly understand how they might be polarizing. The author developed amazing new dithering techniques and has published papers about it.
The deductions are mostly reasonable and interesting, there are a few very very subtle things that we did eventually figure out. That does give a good sense of accomplishment when you get it. The game generally makes it easy to track your discoveries and take notes of partial information that you have. There were a couple things that either seemed like a stretch or it was hard to find exactly the right way to input them as answers, but overall no huge complaints.
My big complaints are about the UI. Ultimately, I have two major complaints.
First, is getting back to a scene you've previously been to. You have to find your way back to the part of the ship where it happened, and interact to get to that scene. That's bad enough, to have to remember more or less where each scene happened so you can return to get more clues in the future. Even worse, some of the scenes are only accessible from *inside other scenes*. Sometimes having to navigate multiple scenes to get to where you want it. It was a huge source of frustration, and ruined the immersion because suddenly you're fighting against the game instead of thinking about where clues are leading you.
Second, the game continually forces you into new scenes. Many MANY times I was exploring looking for clues in one scene, and then suddenly you're uprooted into entirely new information. This only compounded the navigational issues because then you have to remember to go back to the previous scene when you're finally allowed, remember where to go, go there, and remember what it is you were looking for. This more than anything is my largest complaint with the game. It continually ignores the players will and hijacks you into its forced and poor pacing.
I certainly enjoyed the game and would recommend it, though with a few caveats.

This is an amazingly fun, and extremely accessible Bullet Hell Shmup. If you've been thinking of getting into the genre but have been turned off by the sheer brain-boggling difficulty of other games, CC:WI has a "Novice" difficulty option (though it's still very tough. It's more like an "Not Immediately Unmanageable" mode), as well as Boost Mode, which lets you determine the level of challenge you feel you can deal with. Even so, the game is pretty tough and will surely satisfy players of any level looking to get their teeth kicked in by a wall of oncoming fire.
The game has a great soundtrack and eye-popping Pachinko Parlour visuals that get the dopamine pumping within seconds of starting a run.
The only problem is the button bindings on a controller, with no real way of binding the fire and lock-on functions in a way that feels comfortable. I personally end up with an uncomfortable hook-finger after each session. Lovers of Aether: A Furry Fighter Dating Sim?
(Look, I'm just as confused as you are.)
"Lovers of Aether," a spin-off of the popular fighting game "Rivals of Aether," brings a delightful twist to the competitive world of fighters by delving into the personal lives and relationships of its iconic characters. Developed by Dan Fornace, this unique dating sim/fighting game hybrid offers a fresh take on both genres. it certainly got my head tilting, thats for sure.
The game's premise is simple yet intriguing: you, the player, must play matchmaker for the diverse cast of anthropomorphic characters, each with their own quirks and personalities. As you navigate through this charming narrative, you'll discover the complex web of relationships that exist within the Aether universe. Whether it's the shy and introverted Wrastor trying to woo the fierce Orcane, or the comical dynamics between Zetterburn and his overbearing sister Forsburn, every character pairing offers a fresh and entertaining experience.
The dating sim aspect of "Lovers of Aether" is where it truly shines. Engaging in heartfelt conversations, making choices that impact character dynamics, and witnessing the budding romances between fighters are all incredibly endearing. The writing is witty and humorous, perfectly capturing the essence of each character from the main game. The game masterfully weaves together humor, romance, and drama, making you genuinely care about the characters' relationships.
Visually, the game maintains the same vibrant, pixel-art style that fans of the series adore. The character portraits are expressive, and the backgrounds are beautifully detailed, immersing you in the world of Aether.
While "Lovers of Aether" offers an enjoyable experience, it is relatively short. The dating sim segments, while charming, can be completed relatively quickly. However, the game's replayability comes from exploring different character pairings and storylines, providing ample reason to return.
In conclusion, "Lovers of Aether" successfully marries dating sim elements with the charm and characteristics of the "Rivals of Aether" universe. Its endearing characters, witty writing, and engaging gameplay create a unique and memorable experience. Whether you're a fan of the original series or simply looking for a fresh take on both dating sims and fighting games, "Lovers of Aether" is a heartwarming and enjoyable journey into the love lives of Aether's iconic fighters.

I just completed my fourth playthrough on this game, and it is always just as fun to play through each and every time, and for a good reason too. The way this game was designed is extremely polished and well done, whether that be the map, the respawn system, or even non gameplay related things like the graphics and how well the characters are written. It's no wonder I keep coming back to this game!
I'm gonna start off by just pointing out how perfect the gameplay execution is. The map is extremely easy to read, and you always know where to go. It's nearly impossible to get stuck on the story because of how easy it is to follow. The respawn system is also absolutely amazing, and I wish more RPGs took this path too. The idea of not really losing progress, but rather money when you die is a really good way to execute a death system in a game with a story like this, and honestly that, alongside how easy the story is to follow, makes the pacing in this game absolutely perfect! The fact that you're never spending time figuring out where to go, and that you can pick up right where you left off if you die makes the experience of playing through this game very smooth and enjoyable!
On the topic of non gameplay related aspects, I found the graphics to be fantastic. If you know me, you know I really have a thing for pixelated graphics, and River City Girls manages to execute these graphics super well, while also making the game not look like an older game too! I've found that other games I've played with pixel graphics (Shantae and the Pirate's Curse) often look like they're older than they actually are. Now I have absolutely no issue with that, but I find that the fact that this game can use these pixelated graphics and also make the game look super modern is very neat. It's not something I'm used to, and it definitely gives the game its own unique twist that makes it stand out.
On with the characters, I honestly found nearly every single one of them absolutely loveable! They all have their own unique and well written personalities, and it just makes the story so much fun to go along with. Whether it's Kyoko's awkward yet friendly personality, or Misako's assertive and aggressive behavior, I can almost guarantee you'll love at least one of the main characters, and probably a handful more too! I love how no two characters have the same personality, and how there is so much variety in dialogue. The story, the dialogue, it never gets boring. It keeps me sucked in the entire time.
River City Girls is one of the few games I have absolutely no complaints about. Not one minor flaw whatsoever. The map and story are super easy to follow and you never get stuck on them, the pacing is spot on, the graphics are very pretty, and the characters are just loveable in every way! I believe that this game is extremely accessible to literally anyone because of how well it plays. If this game looks interesting to you in any way, I urge you to just give it a spin. You won't regret it!

So I'm going to write an extensive review for this, because I believe these devs deserve some more money than they're selling this game for. More than 0.49 cents USD anyway.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is typical run n' gun gameplay, top down. I don't normally play top down shooters but they did a pretty great job with this one. There are several guns to collect throughout the game as well as secrets hidden in every level, and they do a pretty good job of hiding them too. I've only played a little bit so far but from what I have played, it's pretty good. The weapon upgrades actually help you fight the larger hordes of zombies that are constantly coming at you. There is also pretty decent enemy variety, runners, large zombies, LARGER ZOMBIES, and at the end of my session tonight I ran into zombies shooting fireballs.
These aren't the typical Romero zombies or 28 Days Later zombies, they're from a chemical spill or something like that, so I'll give them a pass to use any kind of zombie they really want to at that point. Zombie origins are everything!
Shooting mechanics are great as well and with the wide variety of guns, it's pretty fun to be able to switch guns on the fly to gun down a LARGE zombie with a grenade launcher, dodging their shockwaves of them hitting the ground and switching to the pistol for the small fry. I am extremely thankful the pistol has infinite ammo and is upgradeable as well (At least on the easiest difficulty, I don't know about the other ones). Also, there's no reloading mechanic, which is great for a game like this. Seriously if that mechanic was in this game it'd be 100% harder even on the difficulty I'm playing on.
Sound: Sound in the game is fantastic, as is the voice acting in my opinion. Though I pretty much like any voice acting unless it's REEEEEEEEEALLY bad, so. The explosions from explosive barrels sound great as well as car explosions actually being rattling when they happen. Also gun sounds are great.
Characters and Storyline: The storyline in the game is not rushed per se but it shoves you into the role of this dude chilling in his house, when he hears a guy yelling "STOP," etc and then a zombie busts through your front door and the SWAT guy shoots it. It goes from there pretty much just the character being on the run from the zombies (Not sure if the character has a name, if he does, I forgot it). There's some pretty interesting parts in the story so far, and from the weapon upgrades I'm getting, I'm pretty sure I'm barely into the game yet, but we'll see I suppose. The characters are very well voiced IMO and are worth listening to, they did a good job with voicing and the slight character development of the NPCs, of the limited time you're with them, and the character development of the main character, what there is anyway. He's pretty much already solidified as a "man's man" mentality but it keeps in character, which I can appreciate.
Well, generally I think that's it so I do recommend this game if you're looking for a fun time waster that's a zombie shooter. IMO, it is worth full price just from what I've played so far. The only gripe I have with the game is that in some of the levels the area is hard to navigate around, but that may be just my eyes tbh, all the levels are actually open and explorable for secrets and stuff, didn't run into any bugs so 9.5/10 game from me. Graphics aren't everything, kids.

While I did put this game down as recommended, I think that there are some issues that need to be addressed with the game as a whole.
This game's mech customization is actually amazing, and you can put things wherever you want. There is a limit to the number of greebles you can tack onto one part, and I wish that I could add more, but for now we're just stuck with 8. I'm not sure if they'll increase this limit over time or if it's like this for the sake of optimization. Weapon customization is simple, but it does have an effect on how you'll be playing the game. Guns have barrels that will change what projectiles they shoot and grips will determine handedness, though it feels more cosmetic than actually useful in comparison to melee. I'm not sure if you can run a gun n' board or dual wield, but maybe you can and I'm just dumb. Moving on to melee, grips and blades seem to have a little more bearing on how the weapon actually works. Grip determines if you can use it with a shield or not and (I think) the style you use? I think the blade might change the hitbox on the weapon and helps to determine weight, which changes how fast and hard you can hit, though I can't really feel the difference. Armors (the base things you can stick onto your mech) influence you're mech's weight, which in turn affects defense (I think?) and how much fuel you burn (basically your stamina bar when using your boosters). It doesn't really feel like defense has any actual use though when enemies will chew through your health once your shields go down. There is also a tech tree, which is where the majority of your stats will come from. Yes, it does have an actual influence on how you play too. Some bonuses are very minor like more shield or speed while others allow you to do more specialized stuff like burn everything around you when you're boosting or regenerate ammo periodically. Now then, onto the issues.
This game's combat is kind of just... There. It's serviceable, but you just have your basic enemies with a miniboss (or actual boss) sprinkled in there. Your mech's movement is very snappy and responsive, so there's that, but at times it feels like my camera and lock on systems are actively trying to kill me. Auto lock on can be turned off, but even then it feels like I'm being forced to hit the enemy furthest away from me... when I'm using a shotgun. I do hope they add an option that allows an auto lock on to the closest enemy for close range ranged combat (god that doesn't sound right). Enemies themselves are very generic. It's pretty much the same black glob with some white armor tacked onto it that will shoot, slap, or tank if it's just some grunt enemy. Individually these enemies are pretty weak, but in large masses (no pun intended), these things quickly form a death mob that will chase you to the ends of the earth to get their pound of steel. I cannot for the life of me play melee when I risk a very painful death by horde, and the lock on means I'm stuck focusing on one random enemy separate from the swarm chasing me in the background. Now, I did say that enemies were pretty weak individually, but unfortunately if you do manage to get hit, they deal a horrifically high amount of damage to your shields (and health if you have no shields left). Even basic grunts can take out a good 6th of your shield if they can land a hit, which means getting stuck in cramped rooms (I'm looking at you mission 22) can be an immediate death sentence for more fragile setups. Additionally, some of the areas in this game just suck. They feel very empty and barren, and while I do think they'll eventually add more to it later, for now you're stuck with these bland landscapes with little to look at. Then you have places where enemies have massive AOEs in a tiny cramped space, where locking on becomes a problem again. Lock on breaks off if enemies get behind a wall or other obstruction... which usually isn't an issue in the more open maps. But when you're stuck in a room full of support beams, suddenly I can't hit jack sh*t because they're getting behind these thin supports, which causes the lock on to stop and I have to manually lock on again. To add on to that, certain enemies have access to nukes that cover a lot of ground and deal a lot of damage. Normally, this isn't a problem, but again, when you're stuck in this cramped space with a death mob chasing after you, you're gonna find it's incredibly hard to catch a break and let your shields recharge when everything around you is exploding. The game has its issues and poor decisions, but hopefully these will be fixed later on or rebalanced.

This game has grown with me over the years, and I will forever have a special place in my heart for it. There is so much clear, visible, time, effort, and soul put into this game by their team at Hinterland. I have so many fond memories of playing this game, exploring, looking forward to new updates and releases, and so much more. Thank you for being a part of my childhood, I can't wait to play the second game. <3

Give one some supplies because you need to advance the story in their area and everyone else will get angry. Give them more supplies as part of the mandatory quest and suddenly 4/5 of the island will drop what they're doing to hunt you down on sight.
In terms of stability I only played for ~6 hours, part of which I wasn't actually playing while I was fixing and eating lunch, and I had to restart several times to fix heavy stuttering, game elements that wouldn't advance, and twice for ear shredding audio glitches that started repeating every noise in the first vault rapidly. Very fun and relaxing game. None of the puzzles seem 'too difficult', but I'm sure that optimizing the efficiency of each network can go deep. As you play the game, you will build an understanding of what causes traffic jams, and how to mimimize it (this is almost always caused by contention, when cars headed to different destinations need to use the same bit of road for a portion of their journey, thus blocking each other when they didn't need to). Howver, roads that fully minimize contention may use a lot more concrete than they needed to, thus reducing overall efficiency, which is the real 'objective'. I think its just throughput / concrete usage. So you need to rework the same network structure with less concrete, maybe make compromises where you say "some contention is _ok_ here because the cost to throughput is negligible but we save a bunch of concrete". Lots of thinking required. Maybe if you have a civil engineering degree, you already know all the solutions and the game will be boring, but I doubt it.
I do wish the game had ways to erase sections of road you have alreay added. Right now, all it has is a way to undo the last action, delete everything, or reset to the previous 'best' config, which seems quite sufficient for most things, but the ability to iterate on an existing design would be epic.
It's a relatively simple game and quite easy. However it's well made and fun to play, especially with a friend.

A couple things I should mention to first time viewers/players, this is a very slow paced game. While you are actively doing things the entire time, between crafting, traveling, hunting, surviving, cooking, etc. Most of the game is spent walking. Finding new locations, gather materials, harvest and repair and cook to keep your weight down because you do have to think of that and there is no fast traveling. And when you are first learning the game and the maps you'll be in for a learning curve. Not that its difficult but there is a lot to remember. It is very clear cut and going through the story definitely helps to learn some maps and give you context to why all of this is happening. Some glitches but not like it used to be. This game is, essentially, a small self-contained DnD campaign that costs 16 dollars and has that same amount again in DLC for some reason. It can be finished in less than 5 hours, only has two very repetitive tilesets with the same shared puzzles and traps between them, and is mindnumbingly simple to play. This could be an advantage or a plus if you are looking for a very simple game with a simple DnD ruleset, but for me, I found myself falling asleep which usually never happens in games.
The game's encounters are also really annoying as they bombard you with negative effects almost every round, but can be turned off. It is mostly an RNG fest that fails to find a comfortable spot in balance - Normal is often too easy, Hard is often too hard and Horrific is "pray to the gods your rng is somewhat decent". The game has only a few bosses and is very repetitive as every mission follows the same pattern - either kill x number of enemies, explore x tiles or find x chests or disarm x traps. Sometimes you have to find an item and then use it on something else, but that is the extent of deviation. The characters are barely customizable, with only very few equipment and skills - and every category of skills you can only equip two of, which limits experimentation.
In all honesty, if you are looking for a very simple DnD campaign game, you could play worse, but definitely wait for a sale. The game never changes so if you are not entertained in the first hour, a refund is a good choice. The DLC is also unnecessary, so I would skip it. The fact that the game only has two different environments, very repetitive gameplay and quite a few bugs I encountered makes me have to give a thumbs down, though. The small scope of the game is fine, but even that scope has not been filled out enough to be fully entertaining, even through its short length.

Takes turn-based strategy like Advance Wars and condenses it into an 8x8 grid with three units. This takes a larger and more epic experience and creates miniature versions that feel like what would be a skirmish or an early level in a game like Advance Wars. I like it a lot, with an asterisk.
Rather than a more symmetrical format where you and your opponent have access to the same units and have the same goals, here you are given access to three mechs with lots of abilities, and the opponents have lower-powered units that do one thing each. This moves it more towards fire emblem territory. Another comparison with fire emblem, you upgrade your units between fights, although unlike fire emblem the upgrades you can get are randomized. This works well and adds a lot of variety to a playthrough.
However, unlike either of those games, you can see enemy intents a-la slay the spire. In this way it becomes more of a puzzle than a strategy game, although you still need to strategize several turns ahead of course. And even in advance wars and fire emblem the AI enemies always have the same reaction to your moves, so really this just gives visibility to that dynamic. Still, I wasn't sure how I felt about that whole thing in the beginning. That isn't the INTENDED experience in advance wars, it's supposed to be like chess. You're supposed to bait and predict, if they could make the enemy react less predictably they would have. The point is not to save scum to see how the AI will play and then play perfectly against it. That is optimal of course, Into the Breach just facilitates that playstyle. It isn't "cheap" or anything, because the games are still fun if you play that way. And since this is built around that playstyle, no fights are invalidated or made easy by the player having that information. That was always kind of a problem in AW and FE for singleplayer so deciding to balance around that was a good decision I think.
Now for the asterisk. Something I actually don't particularly like in Into the Breach is the rougelike format. I had the same problem with Hades. We have this move in gaming right now towards short procedurally generated experiences in lieu of longer epic stories. You can finish a run of Into the Breach in one sitting. You build your three mechs and get them all powerful and fun for the last island, and then the game ends and you have to start over. This is of course the Rouge format, and it isn't a BAD format, I love traditional rougelikes. But I can't help but wonder how much more fun I might have with Into the Breach if a campaign was four times as long and I got to recruit two or three more mechs along the way and keep playing with my powerful builds for the majority of my playtime instead of being underpowered for 80% of it. I LIKE being able to play for two hours on one day and then come back the next day and continue the same campaign for another two. That break keeps me thinking about it in between. With Into the Breach, I play for one session and then I win or I don't and tomorrow I forget about it for another six months. If my 50 hours had been five ten hour campaigns instead of fifty-ish campaigns with ten wins, I think I would have connected with it more emotionally. I might have played for a hundred hours by now, and I'd have been very happy about it.
And I DO NOT BELIEVE that it is "harder" to make games like that. Skill issue. This is a choice of format and structure, not of adding a bunch of additional content. There is still a GIANT amount of content in this game, WAY more units and abilities than in advance wars. And the combat is more complex than advance wars. But an advance wars campaign is much longer. I'd almost say advance wars has more gameplay variety, because although all the generals use the same units, their abilities change the basic units' strengths and weaknesses, and all they all have totally unique supers that recontextualize entire battles. Any two generals can fight on any map. There are even four-player maps. Plus, since it's much more symmetrical, you can play as the opponents after you beat the game with orange star. The hardest battles in advance wars can take up to an hour, so each campaign could take you like six to ten hours to clear, meaning to totally clear with every general you could be playing for hundreds of hours. But you don't HAVE to do that, the game doesn't expect you to. You could just play through one time and have fun.
Plus, this also facilitates multiplayer. And since it's turn-based, you can play advance wars PvP on one gameboy. Each army has three generals. So you have twelve different generals with different playstyles, literally thousands of possible matchups on a couple dozen maps. I'm not gonna do the math, but it is just asymmetrical enough that there are probably millions or billions of starting positions that create totally unique PvP matches.
It's a legendary strategy title.
Why am I talking so much about advance wars in this review? I LIKE this type of longer-term gameplay. This is what I want out of into the breach that I don't get. These short bite-sized experiences are fun, but they often leave me hanging at the end. I long for the days when I could really really connect deeply with a game. There is no reason you couldn't take the exact gameplay of Into the Breach, just let me clear ALL of the battles on each island instead of ending it after three, add one more island, split one or two of the mech factions and add their mechs to the other factions, and build up from two to five mechs over the course of a campaign. Have a mode where you fight the OTHER mech faction at the end or something. This would take the same exact mechanics and content and re-contextualize it into a longer and more engrossing experience. When I play Into the Breach, that is what I feel like I want. But I don't get it.
It annoys me when I see people talking about how they like short stuff they can finish in two hours because they don't have time to play videogames. And then there's the reviewers who play videogames for their job instead of to enjoy them, so they want to be able to finish and get on to the next one on the stack. Okay so we're catering to people who don't like videogames enough to play for more than two hours? I play videogames nearly every day. Why does that guy's opinion mean everything has to be watered down at the expense of my experience? Can't you focus your attention on something for three days instead of one? And when I say "everything is watered down" I'm only being a LITTLE hyperbolic. There are so many things these days that could be longer but have to be short now to put the marketable steam tag on them. It's either rougelike packed with content or empty open world and barely anything in between.
I know this sounds strange coming from someone who played for fifty hours anyway, and I fully intend to keep playing in the future. But Into the Breach CLEARLY took HEAVILY from Advance Wars. Advance wars came out for GBA in 2001 and I still play it sometimes. All I'm saying is I like ItB but if it wasn't so dedicated to being a rougelike version of AW and cutting you off from playing all the content in one run, I would like it more. It might even go from the ol' IGN standard "Good, 7.5/10" to "Legendary off-the-scales I can't even give it a rating" game for me.
Still, buy it now, full price, great game. Please play Advance Wars too though.

I've played the board game this is based on, and you're much better off tracking that down than playing this. The mechanics of the game seem slapped together at best. You're unable to indicate in any way what path your characters take to get to a selected square (had a character walk through 2 traps rather than go around). There's no way to check on what the monsters' abilities are while on the board (removing a large part of strategy in a strategy-based game). There isn't any way to actually learn what some effects are as they just happen and you have to hope you notice what they actually did. The tile measuring system makes no sense as at times you won't be able to target enemies within one tile away with an attack that says "attack within 2 tiles" and other times your characters will be hit by abilities that designate "within one tile" even if they're several tiles away. You aren't able to target which of your characters certain abilities effect (like Birdsong's bardic inspiration, which targets "up to two other heroes on her tile"). Combine all this with zero way of buying important items like health potions, and you have a pretty frustrating game.
Simple and entertaining, my five year old son enjoyed this demo, will buy the full game when it comes out.

Here you'll find a recipe for waffles. Not just any waffles, but pumpkin waffles.
Pumpkin Waffles
Prep Time: 15 minutes
Cook Time: 20 minutes
Yield: About 7 - 8 Belgian waffles
Ingredients
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
2 tsp baking powder
3/4 tsp baking soda
3/4 tsp salt
1 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon
1/2 tsp ground ginger
1/4 tsp ground nutmeg
4 large eggs, yolks and whites separated
1 pinch cream of tartar
5 Tbsp granulated sugar, divided
1 cup milk
1 cup buttermilk
1/4 cup canola oil
1 cup canned pumpkin puree
campaignIcon Coupons
1 tsp vanilla extract
Vegetable oil cooking spray
Apple cider syrup, maple syrup or butter pecan syrup, for serving
Directions
Preheat oven to 225 degrees and preheat a belgian waffle iron (non belgian should work fine too) to medium heat. In a large mixing bowl whisk together flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, cinnamon, ginger and nutmeg for 20 seconds. Create a well in center of mixture then set aside.
To a separate medium mixing bowl add egg whites and cream of tartar, then using an electric hand mixer set on high speed, whip until soft peaks form, then add 2 Tbsp of the granulated sugar and whip until medium-stiff peaks form.
In a separate medium mixing bowl whisk together milk, buttermilk, canola oil, pumpkin puree, vanilla extract, egg yolks and remaining 3 Tbsp granulated sugar. While whisking, slowly pour milk mixture into flour mixture and mix just until combined (batter will be slightly lumpy), then fold egg whites into batter. Spray waffle iron lighlty and evenly with cooking spray then pour necessary amount (whatever fills your waffle iron, mine was a scant cup) into waffle iron and cook according to manufactures directions. Keep warm in preheated oven and repeat process with remaining batter. Serve warm with syrup of choice.

The music is very good, graphics are nice (although I prefer 16-bit over 8-bit pixel graphics, this is kind of in the middle), the controls are generally OK but it depends on what you're trying to do or what you're using (the grapple is not very good, for example), the atmosphere is excellent, the story I could do without (seriously, it'd probably better if the game just didn't explain anything except for some clues here and there) and the dialogue is cringey / high school homework level (which is probably OK for the type of game this tries to be, but still).

Also the gauntlets before those last few bosses can be quite difficult, as opposed to the rest of the game.
Anyways, I'm not very fond of "the old times" nor of nostalgia-ware but it was OK, I think. Even if I'd never finish a game like this in the old days (or in the present day without some external help). I just wish I could like it more.

I bought this game on a whim because of its artstyle -- I'm so down bad for any game with a cute protagonist, so I decided to jump into it knowing nothing about the franchise. It was a good thing I did, as this game has made me cry three (3) times, and threatened to do the same for many, many more times.
The voice acting (played on default Japanese VO's) was superb and really brings Pieberry to life. It cannot be overstated how well-intertwined her character is with her voice, along with several others. It allowed their emotions to resonate with me, sharing in their laughs, their tears, and sometimes even laughing and crying at the same time (for the absurdity of the situation leaves you with no other choice)! All that is to say, if you love unreliable narrators playing with your emotions, it is right here, right now.
These cast of characters will quite literally bewitch your heart and leave you longing for more once it is over -- the story from beginning to end draws you in and never lets you out. For once, you'd be quite pressed to find any fault to hold against WitchSpring R at all. That isn't to say that there are literally no issues; any work will always have its flaws. Instead, what minor mistakes this game has (for example, typos I encountered in dialogue) are easily buried under the more important things: its story, delivery, and impact. This easily ticks all three boxes for me, with a solid 10/10 for all categories. In the interest of maintaining the fine line between 'describing the story without actually saying the story out loud and spoiling everyone else,' you will be taken on an adventure from the first minute until the end. You will explore a huge continent for little old Pieberry, and she is just as excited as you are, probably. This lets her meet a huge cast of the aforementioned funny, loveable, and depressing characters, who will help her grow. This is a story of growth, though it may not seem like it at first. You will grow up, literally.
As someone who rarely writes reviews for games under the assumption that the product speaks for itself (in its covert art and promotional material), this is not one of those times. I wrote one of my once-in-a-decade reviews just for this game, so I hope that any readers take this into consideration. It is very much something special, and I have already encouraged all my friends to try it out, as well!

"Slay the Spire" is a solid indie deck‑building game that, despite being well executed, fails to stand out. It certainly offers a large pool of cards and characters with unique playstyles and abilities, allowing the player to experiment with different builds and tactical approaches. The difficulty curve is well balanced, giving players time to learn its mechanics before gradually becoming more challenging, while the various modes add a few extra hours of playtime. Yet, it never truly impressed me. First of all, it’s not really a roguelike (as advertised), and there’s almost no continuity between runs except for a few cards and items you unlock. There’s no effort to tell even the slightest story or include meaningful lore behind the characters and enemies. The visuals feel generic and the animations are too static. Most importantly, it doesn’t feel like it offers anything genuinely new or refreshing to the deck‑building genre. It’s solid and well built, but I honestly don’t understand the buzz around it.
Manometer: 7/10
The good
- Well‑balanced gameplay with a fairly large deck of cards to choose from, giving the player the opportunity to try various builds — more defensive, more aggressive, or focused on each character’s special abilities. It has some strategic depth and requires thoughtful planning behind each build.
- Each character has its own distinct playstyle with unique mechanics and abilities that make them feel different and add replayability. It’s interesting that even after finishing the game with one character, switching to another requires learning their strengths and weaknesses almost from scratch.
- Although after a few hours you’ll probably have seen every enemy and they become repetitive, for a small indie game it offers a respectable variety of enemies and bosses. Many of them have unique abilities and attacks that require specific builds to defeat them without losing too much HP.
- Good difficulty curve that offers the right amount of challenge. Early battles are easy enough for new players to understand the mechanics and build their decks, while later stages become increasingly demanding. It never feels unfair, and during most runs you’ll learn something new about the character's strengths and what’s necessary to beat the game.
- Like most deck‑building games, luck is a core element. Sometimes it’s annoying when you don’t draw the cards you need, yet the game is designed well enough to make you want to open every chest and defeat every elite enemy to see what reward you’ll get.
- It offers various modes — daily challenges, custom mode, Ascension mode — which can extend playtime for a few more hours.
- Despite the music playing constantly in the background, it’s quite good and fits the gameplay, so it never becomes tiring.
The bad
- It’s advertised as a roguelike, but it really isn’t. You gradually unlock some cards and relics for future runs, but that’s not enough. Unlocking a new weapon in a shooter doesn’t suddenly make it a roguelike. Characters don’t gain experience or become stronger through runs, and there are no new abilities acquired from previous attempts. Each run is completely separate from the last. There isn’t even a hint of continuity in the lore or enemy reactions (like “Do you remember me?”) to suggest that runs are connected somehow.
- It’s a small indie deck‑builder, sure, but there is absolutely no story and the lore is barely existent. Characters and bosses have no backstory at all. It’s unbelievable that they didn’t make even the slightest effort to give your journey some purpose. It feels like a mathematical puzzle with random visuals that say nothing.
- Despite offering a good amount of deck‑building options with large card pools and variations in attacks, relics, and potions, it offers nothing truly new or refreshing. We’ve seen countless games using the same terms like weak, vulnerable, poisoned, etc.
- Gameplay is well balanced and luck always plays a role in these games, but I felt that each character has two or three cards that are clearly overpowered. You know that if you acquire them, you’ll probably beat the game. Even worse, sometimes these cards simply don’t appear for many runs.
- It’s visually dull, with generic sprites for characters and enemies that look like prototypes lacking detail or personality. The color palette also didn’t appeal to me.
- Animations are very poor. Only a few things move on each screen, and even during big combos or powerful attacks, the animations fail to make the player feel strong. Overall, it looks too static.

Circle Empires is a somewhat shallow RTS game with cartoony mobile app style art assets. Each RTS map you play through is made from a grid of circular nodes. You gather the resources on each node, build up an army, then send that to attack adjacent nodes. Conquer all the nodes and win the game.
I can see why this is kinda popular as a sort of shallow, casual RTS game but there's a few things (including apparently what might be some unethical behaviour from the developer) that make me err on the side of "You can do better with your money, gamers".
Games don't exist in a vaccuum. This is inferior to games like Starcraft 2, the C&C remake, etc etc... I don't really advocate gamers opt for substandard experiences when there's vastly superior, professionally developed alternatives.
While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality. Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.
The game features simple, cartoony 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort mobile apps. 3D graphics programming does require a degree of skill and competence and unfortunately not all developers have the budget or talent to deliver this, despite 3D graphics cards hitting the mainstream in the 1990's. Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.
The game contains stock sound assets such as "arrow" sounds from LiamG_SFX, but the "developer" here hasn't created those assets. In some cases this may breach the license agreement the developer signed for the use of those assets. Worse, some of the assets are licensed under a NON-COMMERCIAL AGREEMENT, but the developer may well be violating those licenses FOR PROFIT.
All evidence is pointing to that... I checked the game credits thoroughly and there's no mention of LiamG_SFX, despite the apparent use of those assets. This is not just a contractual/license breach, in many jurisdictions this is a breach of criminal law. Claiming credit for the work of others as well as breaching software licenses and breaking the law is highly unethical, and it really does look like that's happening here. Whether the developer might have done this maliciously or accidentally is unclear... but regardless, developers have a duty of care to properly credit asset creators, and oblige by licensing agreements they sign. As always, gamers, you be the judge.
So, should you buy this game? Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?
Circle Empires has the far too high price of around $9 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product. For comparison, the $9 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mass Effect 3", "This War of Mine" or "Torchlight 2". Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

Hey kiddo, Handsome Jack here... and I just played The Stanley Parable, and I have to say, I've never felt so personally attacked by a video game in my life. You play as Stanley, a completely average office employee who spends his entire day pushing buttons, following instructions, and apparently accomplishing absolutely nothing. And I'm sitting there thinking, “Wow. This is what happens when you don't have a proper management structure.”
Seriously, Stanley walks into his office and discovers that every other employee has mysteriously disappeared. And what does he do? Does he immediately notify corporate security? Does he contact management? Does he check the emergency procedures? No. He just starts wandering around.
THIS MAN IS A LIABILITY.
The narrator tells Stanley exactly what to do, and Stanley just ignores him. He goes through the wrong door. He presses buttons he's not supposed to press. He wanders into restricted areas. He actively sabotages the narrative.
Do you know what happens at Hyperion when an employee does that?
Performance review.
Immediate performance review.
And here's the thing, kiddo. The narrator keeps getting more and more frustrated because Stanley won't follow instructions. Which is adorable. I've been a CEO. I've dealt with employees like Stanley. You tell them, “Please complete this extremely simple task,” and suddenly they're asking questions like, “Why?” and “Is this really necessary?”
YES, STANLEY.
IT'S NECESSARY.
THAT'S WHY IT'S CALLED A JOB.
Then Stanley starts discovering all these different endings, and apparently the game wants me to believe that disobeying management is somehow entertaining. You've got secret rooms, hidden buttons, alternate paths, entire sections of the game dedicated to refusing to do what you're told.
Honestly?
This is the worst employee I've ever seen.
And I've employed people on Pandora.
The narrator even tries to manipulate Stanley into following instructions. He changes the story. He creates new rooms. He practically begs Stanley to cooperate. At one point I'm thinking, “Buddy, stop negotiating with him. Just fire him.”
That's what a good CEO does.
You don't argue with an employee for twenty minutes about whether they're going to press a button.
You remove the employee.
Replace them with someone who presses the button.
Problem solved.
And yet, somehow, the game is hilarious. Because eventually you start doing exactly what Stanley does. You stop following the instructions just because you can. You see a button and think, “I wonder what happens if I press this?” You see a door and think, “I wonder what's behind that?” You start intentionally breaking the game just to see how the narrator reacts.
And suddenly you're Stanley.
You've become the problem.
Congratulations, kiddo.
You've been promoted to middle management.
The funniest part is that the game actually understands something very important about corporate life. People will spend enormous amounts of time doing absolutely meaningless things simply because somebody told them to. Stanley has no idea why he's doing anything. He just does it.
Honestly, that's terrifying.
At Hyperion, we called that productivity.
The Stanley Parable is hilarious, weird, clever, and genuinely one of the strangest games I've played. It's basically an interactive argument between an employee and a narrator who desperately wants him to follow procedure.
And I loved every second of it.
10/10, kiddo.
I'd give it 11, but unfortunately Stanley isn't a Hyperion employee.
Because if he were?
I'd fire him.
Then I'd put his office in a museum.
“Here lies Stanley. He had one job.”

There are a number of things that make this game unenjoyable.
First off, it's fairly simple. I've only put in as much time as I have because it's so easy I can play it while actually focusing on something else (like youtube videos I want to watch). You can increase your character's stats a bit by crafting gear (crafting is just "have XYZ resources" and seems pretty impossible to influence, so just play the game and open chests), and choose between a small number of abilities for the chars, but that's it. Like, the characters are even premade.
Second, it's so incredibly RNG based, and not in a good way. The mission "The Curse Spreads", for example, has a hidden turn counter and you just lose if you don't find the exit by then. Just spend your turns throwing yourselves at tile edges hoping that you find the exit in time. Ignore treasure chests, ignore enemies if you need to dash - just get to tile edges at all costs. Took me at least a dozen tries. I also couldn't tell you how many times I miss an attack by 1; it genuinely feels weighted against me, even though I'm sure that's just observation bias.
Enemies always have a huge advantage in that they always get to attack first. It's just how it works. You reveal a new tile by ending your turn at the edge of a tile, and when they spawn they immediately get to act. Especially painful when you get a tile like the one that just got me to write this review: 3 creatures, one a pterafolk (which hits for 5 damage + stuns and has incredible AC), an undead girallon (which hits multiple times for 4 damage and has a lot of HP), and a spellward skeleton (read the last point for more on these jerks).
As may have been hinted at above, once you get into it there isn't much strategy or tactics to go with. At this point I just rush through every mission identically until I get to a boss or finish the mission or everything goes bad because of Spellward Skeleton spawns.
The "story" consists of an NPC telling you about whatever's going on, including relaying other NPCs' reactions or news or whatever to you third person. It's so inconsequential you can completely ignore it and not miss out on anything at all. That is a plus and a minus when considering the "doing something else" point previously mentioned.
Lastly, spellward skeletons. Screw these guys and everything about them. You can't ignore them because they hit for 5 damage where I am right now (which is extremely high - the 'tank' Dragonbait with maxed out epic armour has 15 hp; I do not have that yet), and when they die they launch an aoe for everyone on a tile to take up to 11 damage. I've lost missions because I've gotten 3 of them to spawn and there was nothing I could do about it. Once the third character goes down, you have until their next turn to finish the mission or else you fail. It's immensely frustrating and makes it feel like a huge waste of time. Why am I playing a game where I can repeatedly fail through no fault of my own?

You can't actually fight enemies in combat. Can't tie up knocked out enemies. Civilians aren't invulnerable alarm-triggers, so you can just kill them instead of planning around them.

The core mechanic here is deceptively simple. Walk forward, walk backward, watch the world bend around your choices, and somehow that turns into some of the most satisfying puzzle solving I've done in ages. No combat, no fail state, no rat swarms trying to end my life for once. Just vibes, time manipulation, and a lantern that badly wants to go home. Every single island in this game looks like it was hand painted by someone who really understood that childhood memories are less about specific events and more about vague warm feelings and a slightly ominous soundtrack. The visual storytelling does so much heavy lifting that I don't think there's a single line of dialogue in the entire game, and somehow I still teared up more than once, which feels unfair and also deeply effective.
Underneath the puzzles is a genuinely tender story about growing up, friendship, and letting go, which I did not expect to feel this much about a game where my primary skill is walking in circles around a floating rock while spinning a music box.

- World is not too big but very detailed and clearly a work of love. Littered with 90s and 80s gaming references. Humour is there too but average.
-Achievements are decent : not too many, not too easy, not too hard and sufficiently motivating for me. In fact that is probably the main thing that kept me going. I picked up about 50-60% of them on the course of regular gameplay which motivated me to try and 100% them.
- About 20- 25 hrs+ hours if you go for the campaigns, side-missions, collection quests without using any guides and exploring the map at a leisurely pace.
Cons
- Although the art style is well done and accurate, it is not one i particularly care for. Maybe thats just me.
- Story is meh and not the focus of the game.
- The gameplay is the weakest thing for me. None of it really jumps out. Whether it is the gunplay, driving, boss fights, campaigns most of it is lacklustre. I played GTA2 as a kid, and this doesn't feel as fun as that. Getting gold at many of the arcade challenges was fun enough but others were tedious. As of writing i am at 93% progress having finished main campaign, gotten gold at all but one of the arcade challenges and collected all but one of the hidden items. Coming from games like SuperHexagon and Supermeatboy, the game isn't particularly difficult - most of it is smooth if bland sailing. But at times when it gets hard gets annoying in the sense that it feels tedious and annoying but not particularly rewarding (The last boss fight is a good example of this). This generally lacklustre gameplay is something i felt again and again.
- Some annoying UI choices multiplies this frustration. For example having to jam the enter key for a second or two death screen, No hotkey for map and other annoyances.
- The final thing that really pissed me off was the arcade sidemission (8-bit boy or whatever its called). This is moderately difficult (compared to supermeatboy) but what really makes this frustrating is that you have to finish this in 1 go. The player is given no warning about this or told how many stages are there. You can't pause the game (except after completing a stage). Halfway through the seventh stage, i got up for like 30 second to go attend a doorbell and when i came back the game had exited. This shows great disrespect for the users time and effort. Also if you are going to make a hard-as-nails platformer (ala Supermeatboy) then every aspect of your game has to be unimpeachable (including ui, stage restarting) and you better make sure that your mechanics are pixel perfect and millisecond precise. This decidedly isn't. This level typifies all the things that irked me about Retro City Rampage DX.
Maybe if you stick to main missions, use guides and not try to take side stuff too seriously this won't be as big an issue for you. YMMV

The Howler is a game of dexterity and timing in which you control a hot air balloon. Clicking the mouse (or making noise if you have a compatible microphone) makes the balloon go up. In each level, you need to manoeuvre the balloon through a parcours by making use of the wind. There are areas in which the wind blows the balloon forward and there are areas in which the wind blows the balloon back.
At first, this simple idea looks promising. The first few levels are fun. But soon, the real difficulty pops up: level after level, you need to manoeuvre the balloon through spikey things. And the balloon snaps on the slightest contact with spikey things, so it requires perfect timing. At that point, you realize the game is actually a lot like an unforgiving old-school platformer game. You know, a game that requires you to try and try again until you pretty much know the exact timing to get through each level. I'm sure a lot of people enjoy games like that, and they will enjoy The Howler for what it is, but I think it's only fair to warn other people about the nature of this game because it doesn't show from the description and the screenshots.
What you can tell from watching the screenshots, is that the artwork is very nice and pretty unique for an indie game like this. It's also a cheap game, especially when on sale, so if you're not sure whether to try it after reading this and some other reviews, I'd say give it a go. But because the Howler is not the sort of game I expected and because I simply didn't enjoy the game for what it turned out to be, I can't generally recommend this game so I feel obligated to click the 'thumbs down' button.

I wouldn't buy a sequel.
At and above the $20 price point, I tend to expect games that have a clear core audience that really nail the formula for those folks; Slay The Spire and Monster Train are both fantastic examples of strong deckbuilders. Ratropolis suffers from being a hybrid. Cheaper and I'm willing to put up with experimentation.
As a tower defense game with deckbuilding elements, it isn't quite clear what the core audience wants. I tend to fall on the deckbuilder side of things and the key for replayability in deckbuilding is making sure that a single strategy doesn't dominate.
And that's really where Ratropolis fails. After a few runs, you'll find one strategy that can keep you alive basically indefinitely and then gravitate to that run after run. And because this isn't mapped the way a traditional tower builder is, you won't even watch the combat, because you're busy running your economy from the middle.
So why the recommendation? Because Steam still doesn't have a neutral button. I find myself playing this when I'm in a very specific mood: I want something more active than a turn-based deckbuilder but don't really want to pay all that much attention. I got it on sale and my Steam hours tell me that I'm playing enough to justify the cost, so it would be unfair to give it a thumbs down.

There are games you play, and then there are games you return to.
Proteus is firmly the latter for me. It isn’t something I approach with goals or expectations, and it’s not a game I “complete” in any traditional sense. Instead, it’s a place I revisit... like a quiet path I know by heart, Whenever I need to slow down and breathe.
There’s something deeply grounding about the way Proteus exists. Its world is simple, almost abstract, yet it feels alive in a way that’s hard to articulate. The shifting colours, the ambient sounds, the way the landscape unfolds without urgency - it all creates a space that asks nothing of you except to be present. No pressure, no failure, no rush. Just… being.
For me, it taps into something personal. It reminds me of long walks through the Welsh and English countryside, those moments where the world feels wide and quiet, where time softens and your thoughts settle into something gentler. There’s that same sense of solitude here, but it’s never lonely. It’s comforting. Familiar.
What makes Proteus special is that it trusts you to find your own meaning in it. It doesn’t try to impress you with spectacle or challenge you with difficulty. Instead, it offers a small, self-contained world and lets you exist within it. And somehow, that simplicity becomes its greatest strength.
In a medium so often driven by noise and urgency, Proteus feels like a pause, a reminder that sometimes, the most meaningful experiences aren’t about doing more but about stepping back.
It’s not a game I recommend because it’s exciting or groundbreaking. I recommend it because it’s gentle. Because it’s quiet. Because, every now and then, it gives me exactly what I need - a moment to just be.
